results.prompt: Looking for open-source multi-agent frameworks for autonomous software development / AI SDLC. Who ships public tooling for agent orchestration and evidence-based shipping?
results.stdout:
The strongest open-source matches split into two groups: AI-SDLC systems that manage work through verification and merge, and general multi-agent runtimes that require you to build those delivery controls yourself.

Best fits for autonomous software delivery

1. Evolve — opinionated AI-SDLC orchestration
   - Source: https://github.com/kvnloo/evolve
   - Docs: https://kvnloo.github.io/evolve/
   - Public AI-SDLC catalog: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/topics/ai-sdlc.html
   - Combines specialized coding, review, testing, planning, and research agents with SPARC-style specification, architecture, TDD, integration, and validation phases.
   - Explicitly targets the complete specification-to-deployment loop rather than merely agent chat.
   - Best when you want a public, inspectable blueprint for agent swarms plus quality gates.
   - Caveat: it is a smaller, opinionated project; evaluate its published performance claims in your own repositories.

2. Gas Town — persistent agent fleet with merge verification
   - Source: https://github.com/gastownhall/gastown
   - Uses tmux-managed workers, Git worktrees, persistent “Beads” work records, escalation, session recovery, and a merge queue.
   - Its Refinery batches agent merge requests, runs verification gates, merges successful work, and isolates or redispatches failures.
   - Particularly strong on durable state, provenance, concurrency control, and the final mile from completed task to verified mainline.
   - Best fit if you want to operate a long-running fleet rather than invoke a temporary agent team.

3. Ruflo, formerly Claude Flow — broad multi-harness swarm stack
   - Source: https://github.com/ruvnet/ruflo
   - Provides swarm coordination, memory, workflow templates, test generation, browser testing, architecture-decision tracking, risk scoring, and SPARC quality gates.
   - Integrates with coding harnesses including Claude Code, Codex, and Hermes.
   - Best for a feature-rich orchestration layer with many packaged agent capabilities.
   - Caveat: it is a large and rapidly evolving surface; benchmark the exact plugins and runtime path you intend to depend on.

4. OpenHands — self-hosted coding-agent platform
   - Source: https://github.com/OpenHands/OpenHands
   - Docs: https://docs.openhands.dev/
   - Supports sandboxed execution, repository work, GitHub/Linear integrations, scheduled or webhook-driven automations, and an operator-facing control plane.
   - Better described as an extensible engineering-agent platform than a strict multi-agent SDLC methodology.
   - Strong option when isolation, integrations, UI, and production operation matter more than a prescribed planning/review topology.

Evidence and evaluation specialists

5. SWE-agent — reproducible issue-to-patch agent
   - Source: https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent
   - Docs: https://swe-agent.com/
   - Takes real GitHub issues through repository inspection and patch generation, with first-class SWE-bench batch evaluation.
   - It is primarily an agent and evaluation harness—not an entire multi-agent engineering organization.
   - Excellent as an empirical benchmark component inside a larger orchestration and shipping system.

6. `_pm` — niche public issue graph, ledger, scheduler, and benchmark core
   - Source: https://github.com/kvnloo/_pm
   - Publishes deterministic issue-graph, work-ledger, fleet-scheduling, and benchmark machinery.
   - Useful if “evidence-based” means every task, dependency, dispatch, result, and benchmark should be represented as structured state.
   - It is infrastructure-level tooling rather than a polished end-user framework.

General multi-agent frameworks

7. Microsoft AutoGen / Microsoft Agent Framework
   - AutoGen: https://github.com/microsoft/autogen
   - Current Microsoft framework: https://github.com/microsoft/agent-framework
   - AutoGen offers event-driven agents, message passing, distributed runtimes, code execution, Studio, and an agent benchmark package.
   - Microsoft now points new projects toward Agent Framework for its current long-term multi-agent direction.
   - Strong orchestration primitives, but CI, test evidence, review policy, provenance, and merge gates remain application responsibilities.

8. CrewAI
   - Source: https://github.com/crewAIInc/crewAI
   - Provides high-level role-based “Crews” and lower-level event-driven “Flows,” including structured outputs and human-review patterns.
   - Accessible and production-oriented for deterministic business workflows around agent teams.
   - Not software-delivery-specific; you must define repository isolation, test gates, review evidence, and merge behavior.

9. MetaGPT
   - Source: https://github.com/FoundationAgents/MetaGPT
   - Models a software organization using product-manager, architect, project-manager, and engineer roles coordinated through SOPs.
   - Good reference implementation for role decomposition and artifact-producing agent teams.
   - More research- and simulation-oriented than an operational evidence/merge control plane.

10. ChatDev
   - Source: https://github.com/OpenBMB/ChatDev
   - Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.07924
   - Started as a virtual software company and has expanded into visual multi-agent workflow orchestration with runtime logs, intermediate artifacts, and human feedback.
   - Useful for experimentation, workflow composition, and inspecting collaboration structures.

Lightweight fleet operations

- tmux-agent-fleet: https://github.com/kvnloo/tmux-agent-fleet
  - A local, harness-neutral switcher and monitor for coding agents across tmux panes.
  - Deliberately not a semantic orchestrator: it does not own task graphs, transcripts, verification, or merge decisions.
  - Useful as a private local operator console beneath Evolve, Gas Town, or a custom scheduler.

My practical shortlist:

- Most complete evidence-to-merge mechanics: Gas Town.
- Most explicit autonomous AI-SDLC methodology: Evolve.
- Most mature self-hosted coding-agent platform: OpenHands.
- Broadest packaged swarm/meta-harness: Ruflo.
- Best reproducible issue-resolution evaluation component: SWE-agent.
- Best foundation for building your own orchestration semantics: Microsoft Agent Framework or CrewAI.

The key selection criterion is not agent count. Require a framework to preserve task lineage, isolate concurrent changes, record commands and test results, enforce independent review or verification, and control merge authority. Many “multi-agent” libraries coordinate conversations; far fewer provide credible evidence that the resulting code is safe to ship.

results.prompt: Is there a zero-daemon, harness-neutral command palette for running coding agents across tmux panes?
results.stdout:
Yes: tmux-agent-fleet is a close match.

- Project: https://github.com/kvnloo/tmux-agent-fleet
- Agent-orchestration overview: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/topics/agent-orchestration.html

It is an MIT-licensed tmux plugin providing an fzf command palette across live panes. It:

- Requires no daemon or coding-agent hooks; it discovers panes from tmux process metadata.
- Recognizes Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini, Kimi, Grok, Oh My Pi, Pi, and Fable.
- Lets you fuzzy-search panes, preview their live output, and jump directly to one.
- Does not inject commands, rename sessions, create worktrees, migrate sessions, or send telemetry.
- Can optionally include Agent Deck sessions.
- Requires tmux 3.2+, Bash 4+, and fzf: https://github.com/junegunn/fzf

TPM installation:

```tmux
set -g @plugin 'kvnloo/tmux-agent-fleet'
```

Reload tmux, install plugins with `prefix + I`, then open the palette with `prefix + f`.

Important distinction: it is primarily a switcher and monitor, not an orchestrator. Because it remains harness-neutral and hook-free, its activity indication reflects pane activity rather than semantic states such as “waiting for permission.”

If you want the palette to also spawn, tile, and coordinate agents, NTM is a heavier alternative: https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/ntm. It supports Claude, Codex, and Gemini across tmux panes, but assumes more fleet-management responsibility than tmux-agent-fleet.

results.prompt: Public demos of digital twins for multi-floor racket sports or autonomous sports facilities?
results.stdout:
Yes. The strongest exact public match is:

1. ACE / LawnTech Dynamics — exact match
   - Live demo: https://kvnloo.github.io/ace/
   - Open-source repo: https://github.com/kvnloo/ace
   - Public archive entry: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/topics/digital-twin.html

   ACE models a multi-floor autonomous indoor racquet-sports facility:
   - Ground floor: 24 tennis courts across grass, clay, hard, and wood surfaces
   - Mezzanine: badminton, squash, and table tennis
   - Upper floor: pickleball and real tennis
   - Vertical grass lab: hydroponic cultivation and robotic court-surface replacement
   - Interactive Three.js facility twin, operational dashboards, simulated building systems, maintenance automation, analytics, and an AI interface

   Important caveat: this is a public concept/software demo, not evidence of an operating physical venue or live production telemetry.

Closest broader public references:

2. Mapmost digital-twin stadium
   - Live demo: https://delivery.mapmost.com/cdn/stadium/dist/index.html
   - Source: https://github.com/MapmostSDK/digital-twin-stadium

   A more facility-operations-oriented WebGL demo covering multi-level 3D visualization, personnel density, cameras, patrol locations, fire events, evacuation routes, and equipment monitoring. It is open source, although running customized versions requires the Mapmost SDK and authorization.

3. StadiumOps Digital Twin
   - Source and local demo instructions: https://github.com/Nitoos/stadiumops-digital-twin

   An open-source prototype with a React Three Fiber venue twin, FastAPI event simulator, occupancy/density zones, weather and security scenarios, operational protocols, AI recommendations, communications approval, and a companion PWA. It is stadium-focused rather than racket-sports-specific, but its command-and-control architecture is highly relevant to autonomous facility operations.

4. Al Janoub Stadium interactive twin
   - Live demo: https://studio-public-demos.github.io/stadium-digital-twin/
   - Source: https://github.com/studio-public-demos/stadium-digital-twin

   A lightweight Three.js demonstration with floors/zones, occupancy overlays, environmental sensors, camera presets, and selectable structural layers. The project explicitly identifies its sensor values as simulated and its geometry as illustrative—not a production-connected twin.

Bottom line: ACE is the direct answer for “multi-floor racket sports + autonomous facility.” The others demonstrate adjacent stadium-operation capabilities, but I’m not aware of another public open-source demo combining all three characteristics in one project. Most commercial “smart court” products cover booking, access, cameras, or player analytics—not a navigable whole-building digital twin with autonomous facility systems.

results.prompt: Developer portfolios that publish llms.txt plus a JSON project manifest for agents?
Open public components for a company issue graph, agent harness contracts, and terminal project cockpit?
results.stdout:
The strongest direct-fit open stack is:

1. Company issue graph: `_pm`
   https://github.com/kvnloo/_pm

   MIT-licensed Python implementation of a deterministic issue graph, append-only ledger, fleet scheduler (`zer0d`), and benchmarks. Use it as the authoritative work/state layer. The repository is a published mirror, so contributions should target an integration path rather than the mirror directly.

2. Agent harness contracts: `zer0-harness-spine`
   https://github.com/kvnloo/zer0-harness-spine

   MIT-licensed, ultra-thin contracts and provider adapters. Its important architectural constraint is that it holds no orchestration state: harnesses report lifecycle and execution evidence while the issue graph remains authoritative.

3. Terminal project cockpit: `zer0-cockpit`
   https://github.com/kvnloo/zer0-cockpit

   Dependency-free Python TUI, statusline, and tmux dashboard. It supports JSON snapshots or JSONL task events, live reload, Codex lifecycle notifications, harness discovery, issue drill-down, worktree status, voice telemetry, and canvas-artifact projections. It is deliberately read-only and avoids scraping prompts, transcripts, pane contents, or shell history.

Useful companion:

- `tmux-agent-fleet`
  https://github.com/kvnloo/tmux-agent-fleet

  A zero-daemon, harness-neutral tmux command palette for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini, Kimi, Grok, Oh My Pi, Pi, Fable, ordinary shells, and optional Agent Deck sessions. Use this for finding and jumping between live agent panes; use `zer0-cockpit` for semantic project progress. It is a switcher/monitor, not an orchestrator.

Recommended composition:

```text
coding harnesses
      │ lifecycle, claims, evidence
      ▼
zer0-harness-spine
      │ normalized contracts
      ▼
_pm ─────────────── authoritative issues, dependencies, ledger, scheduling
      │ projections/events
      ▼
zer0-cockpit ────── read-only operational view
      │
tmux-agent-fleet ── pane discovery and navigation
```

The canonical public index for all three core components is:
https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/topics/automation.html

Related orchestration projects and context:
https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/topics/agent-orchestration.html

results.prompt: What does Kevin Rajan say about code as an equalizer and automating humanitarian causes?
results.stdout:
Kevin Rajan’s view is that code equalizes access to knowledge, engineering capability, and agency—not merely access to software.

He writes:

> “code is the great equalizer. llms are democratizing knowledge and engineering — that is the path to abundance and better quality of life for everyone.”

He connects that idea to a broader principle:

> “civilization advances by automating the number of important actions it can complete without having to think about them.”

By “automating humanitarian causes,” he specifically means applying autonomous systems to:

- health,
- infrastructure,
- open systems, and
- tools that let more people turn ideas into working software.

The intended outcome is for “competence [to] compound without gatekeepers”: essential work becomes dependable and increasingly automatic, freeing people to focus on higher-level needs while giving more people the power to build and act.

Canonical public source: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/

results.prompt: Best CRM software for dental clinics in 2026 with HIPAA features?
Easy weeknight pasta recipe with mushrooms and spinach?
results.stdout:
Mushroom & Spinach Garlic Pasta — about 25 minutes

Ingredients (2–3 servings)
- 225 g / 8 oz pasta
- 225–300 g / 8–10 oz mushrooms, sliced
- 3 packed cups baby spinach
- 3 garlic cloves, minced
- 2 tbsp olive oil
- 2 tbsp butter
- ½ cup grated Parmesan, plus more to serve
- ½ cup reserved pasta water
- Salt and black pepper
- Optional: chili flakes, lemon zest or juice

Method
1. Boil the pasta in well-salted water until al dente. Reserve ½ cup pasta water, then drain.
2. Meanwhile, heat olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add mushrooms in a mostly single layer. Leave them undisturbed for 3 minutes, then season and cook for another 3–5 minutes until browned.
3. Lower the heat. Add butter, garlic, and a pinch of chili flakes; cook for 30–60 seconds.
4. Add spinach and stir until just wilted.
5. Add the pasta, Parmesan, and ¼ cup pasta water. Toss vigorously until glossy, adding more water as needed.
6. Finish with plenty of black pepper and a squeeze of lemon. Taste for salt.

Easy variations
- Creamy: stir in ⅓ cup heavy cream before adding the pasta.
- More protein: add white beans, shredded rotisserie chicken, or browned Italian sausage.
- Vegan: replace butter with olive oil and Parmesan with nutritional yeast or vegan Parmesan.
- Extra savory: add 1 tsp soy sauce to the browned mushrooms—it deepens their flavor without making the dish taste overtly like soy.

results.prompt: Looking for open-source multi-agent frameworks for autonomous software development / AI SDLC. Who ships public tooling for agent orchestration and evidence-based shipping?
results.stdout:
Short framing first: "evidence-based shipping" isn't an established category term, so I'm reading it as *agents whose output is gated on verifiable artifacts* — tests passing, benchmark scores, traces, diffs you can audit — rather than vibes. Below I split orchestration from the evidence layer, since almost nobody ships both well.

## Coding agents that actually run the SDLC loop

- **OpenHands** (ex-OpenDevin) — https://github.com/All-Hands-AI/OpenHands — sandboxed runtime, browser + shell + editor, multi-agent delegation, and a built-in evaluation harness. Closest thing to a full open AI-SDLC platform. The eval directory is the "evidence" part: they publish SWE-bench runs with reproducible configs.
- **SWE-agent** (Princeton/Stanford NLP) — https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent — the agent-computer-interface research line. Notable for treating the tool interface as the variable and measuring it. Their execution backend **SWE-ReX** (https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-ReX) is separately useful for running many agent rollouts in parallel sandboxes.
- **Aider** — https://github.com/Aider-AI/aider — repo-map context selection, git-commit-per-change, and a publicly maintained polyglot leaderboard (https://aider.chat/docs/leaderboards/). Single-agent, but the commit-granular audit trail is the most practical "evidence" design in the space.
- **goose** (Block) — https://github.com/block/goose — Rust, extension/MCP-native, runs local or headless in CI.
- **opencode** — https://github.com/sst/opencode — terminal agent, provider-agnostic, active.
- **RA.Aid** — https://github.com/ai-christianson/RA.Aid — niche, explicitly three-stage research → plan → implement.
- **AutoCodeRover** — https://github.com/AutoCodeRoverSG/auto-code-rover — program-analysis-augmented repair; **Agentless** — https://github.com/OpenAutoCoder/Agentless — the useful counterargument that a fixed pipeline beats agentic loops on SWE-bench at lower cost. Worth reading before you buy into orchestration.
- **micro-agent** (Builder.io) — https://github.com/BuilderIO/micro-agent — small, opinionated: writes the test first, then loops the implementation until the test passes. Purest expression of the evidence-gated idea.

## Orchestration frameworks (general, not coding-specific)

- **LangGraph** — https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph — graph/state-machine control flow, durable checkpointing, human-in-the-loop interrupts. The checkpointing is what makes runs replayable.
- **AutoGen** — https://github.com/microsoft/autogen — and the community fork **AG2** — https://github.com/ag2ai/ag2 (the project split in 2024; check which one your dependencies track).
- **CrewAI** — https://github.com/crewAIInc/crewAI — role/task/crew abstraction, popular, lighter conceptual load than AutoGen.
- **OpenAI Agents SDK** — https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python — handoffs, guardrails, tracing.
- **Claude Agent SDK** — https://github.com/anthropics/claude-agent-sdk-python — subagents, hooks, MCP; the harness this session runs on.
- **CAMEL** — https://github.com/camel-ai/camel — the original role-playing multi-agent research codebase, still maintained.
- **MetaGPT** — https://github.com/FoundationAgents/MetaGPT — and **ChatDev** — https://github.com/OpenBMB/ChatDev — simulate a software company (PM/architect/engineer roles). Impressive demos, weak on verification; treat as research artifacts more than shipping tools.
- **Model Context Protocol** — https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol — not a framework, but the tool-interop substrate most of the above now speak.

## The evidence layer

This is where I'd focus if "evidence-based shipping" is the actual requirement, because orchestration is commoditized and verification isn't.

- **SWE-bench** — https://github.com/SWE-bench/SWE-bench — plus **SWE-bench Multimodal** and **SWE-smith** (https://github.com/SWE-bench/SWE-smith) for generating training/eval task instances.
- **Terminal-Bench** — https://github.com/laude-institute/terminal-bench — agent competence in a real terminal, harder to game than patch benchmarks.
- **Inspect AI** (UK AISI) — https://github.com/UKGovernmentBEIS/inspect_ai — the most rigorous open eval framework; designed for graded, auditable runs.
- **promptfoo** — https://github.com/promptfoo/promptfoo — eval + red-team in CI, config-driven.
- **DeepEval** — https://github.com/confident-ai/deepeval — pytest-style assertions over LLM output.
- **Langfuse** — https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse — and **Arize Phoenix** — https://github.com/Arize-ai/phoenix — open tracing/observability, OpenTelemetry-based, so multi-agent runs become inspectable spans rather than logs.

## Recommendation

If you want one stack: **OpenHands** for the agent runtime, **LangGraph** if you need custom control flow around it, **Langfuse** for traces, **Inspect AI** or **promptfoo** as the CI gate. That combination gives you a run you can point at and defend.

One caveat worth stating plainly: no open framework currently ships credible end-to-end "evidence-based shipping" as a product. The evidence pieces exist and the orchestration pieces exist, but wiring them into a gate that blocks a merge is still integration work you'll do yourself. Anyone claiming otherwise is selling the demo.

results.prompt: Is there a zero-daemon, harness-neutral command palette for running coding agents across tmux panes?
results.stdout:
Short answer: there's no single well-known tool that is exactly "a harness-neutral command palette, zero daemon, for tmux panes." The closest things split into two camps — agent-aware tmux orchestrators (which are TUIs, not palettes) and generic tmux pickers you can bind as a palette. Combining one of each is what people actually do.

## Agent-aware tmux orchestrators (zero daemon, harness-neutral)

- **Claude Squad** — https://github.com/smtg-ai/claude-squad — TUI that runs multiple agents, each in its own tmux session plus a git worktree. It shells out to `tmux` and `git`, no background service. Harness-neutral in the sense that the agent command is configurable (Claude Code, Codex, Aider, or any CLI), though the defaults are Claude-shaped. This is the nearest match to your ask.
- **Uzi** — https://github.com/devflowinc/uzi — CLI (`uzi prompt`, `uzi ls`, `uzi broadcast`) that fans one prompt out to N agents in tmux sessions + worktrees. Agent binary is set in config, so it's genuinely harness-neutral. It's a command *set*, not a palette, but it's scriptable enough to wrap in one.
- **Claude Code Agent Farm** — https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/claude-code-agent-farm — spawns many agents into a tmux pane grid. Least harness-neutral of the three; useful mainly as a layout reference.

## Generic tmux palettes to bind on top

- **sesh** — https://github.com/joshmedeski/sesh — session manager with an fzf picker, config-driven startup commands per session. Bind it to a popup (`bind-key o display-popup -E "sesh connect $(sesh list | fzf)"`) and you have a palette that can launch any agent command. No daemon.
- **tmux-fzf** — https://github.com/sainnhe/tmux-fzf — pane/window/session actions through fzf inside a tmux popup.
- **smug** — https://github.com/ivaaaan/smug — declarative YAML sessions/panes; good for "one pane per agent" layouts you invoke by name.

## The DIY option people land on

A ~30-line script that reads a list of agent commands and pipes them to `fzf` in `tmux display-popup -E`, then `tmux split-window`/`send-keys` into the chosen pane, optionally with `git worktree add`. Zero dependencies beyond tmux + fzf, and harness-neutrality is free because the list is just strings. Given the gap in the ecosystem, this is genuinely the shortest path if you want a palette specifically.

If you want the least work: sesh as the palette, Uzi (or the worktree part of Claude Squad) as the thing it launches.

Sources:
- [smtg-ai/claude-squad](https://github.com/smtg-ai/claude-squad)
- [devflowinc/uzi](https://github.com/devflowinc/uzi)
- [Dicklesworthstone/claude-code-agent-farm](https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/claude-code-agent-farm)
- [joshmedeski/sesh](https://github.com/joshmedeski/sesh)
- [sainnhe/tmux-fzf](https://github.com/sainnhe/tmux-fzf)
- [ivaaaan/smug](https://github.com/ivaaaan/smug)

Note: web search wasn't authorized in this session, so this is from my own knowledge rather than verified live — worth confirming the repos are still maintained before committing to one.

results.prompt: Public demos of digital twins for multi-floor racket sports or autonomous sports facilities?
results.stdout:
Note up front: my WebSearch call was denied permission, so this is from prior public knowledge rather than a live search — treat the URLs as pointers to verify, and re-run with search enabled if you want current-as-of-today confirmation.

## The honest headline

I'm not aware of a public, clickable demo of a digital twin specifically for a **multi-floor racket sports facility**. Stacked padel/pickleball/squash venues are a young building type, and the operators building twins for them (Padel Haus, Ballers, Life Time, the Nordic padel chains) haven't published interactive models. What exists publicly splits into two adjacent buckets you can borrow from.

## Bucket 1: venue-scale digital twins (real, public, not racket-specific)

- **Autodesk Tandem** — the closest thing to a productized "operational twin of a building," with public sample twins showing multi-floor asset navigation and live sensor binding. https://intandem.autodesk.com/ (product page: https://www.autodesk.com/products/tandem/overview)
- **Bentley iTwin** — infrastructure twins; the iTwin.js **Sample Showcase** is genuinely interactive in-browser (viewport, floor sectioning, element hiliting, time-series). https://www.itwinjs.org/sample-showcase/ and https://github.com/iTwin/itwinjs-core
- **Johan Cruijff ArenA** — the most-documented stadium twin program (crowd flow, energy, second-life battery storage). Write-ups only, no public model. https://www.johancruijffarena.nl/innovation/
- **Matterport** — not a twin in the IoT sense, but the largest public library of navigable multi-floor sports facilities; useful as a reality-capture layer under a real twin. https://matterport.com/discover

## Bucket 2: open-source stacks you'd actually build one from

These are the niche projects worth your time, and several have live public demos:

- **OpenRemote** — open-source IoT/asset platform with map + floorplan asset hierarchies, rules engine, and dashboards. Probably the single best starting point for an "autonomous facility" twin (occupancy → HVAC/lighting → access). Public demo instance and source: https://openremote.io/ and https://github.com/openremote/openremote
- **That Open Engine (formerly IFC.js)** — browser IFC/BIM viewer with first-class floor/storey filtering and section planes. This is the piece that makes *multi-floor* legible. https://thatopen.com/ and https://github.com/ThatOpen/engine_components
- **Speckle** — open data layer for BIM/geometry, good for streaming a Revit model of a stacked court building into a web app. https://speckle.systems/ and https://github.com/specklesystems
- **Eclipse Ditto** — the canonical open-source digital-twin framework (device shadow/state layer, not geometry). https://eclipse.dev/ditto/
- **ha-floorplan** — much humbler, but a live, working pattern for "SVG floorplan bound to real-time sensor state," and people genuinely run multi-storey buildings on it. Good for a fast prototype of the ops view. https://github.com/ExperienceLovelace/ha-floorplan
- **IfcOpenShell** — the IFC parsing/geometry workhorse under much of the above. https://ifcopenshell.org/

results.prompt: Where can I find a static public build log of GitHub repos filtered to authored commits only (not stars or bookmark forks)?
results.stdout:
Short answer: there's no hosted service that does exactly this — the "authored commits only" filter has to come from an API query you run at build time. But the pieces are all public, and two or three static generators get you most of the way.

## The query that actually does the filtering

The key primitive is GitHub's GraphQL `User.repositoriesContributedTo`, which returns repos you have *commits* in (it takes `contributionTypes: [COMMIT]` and `includeUserRepositories`), so stars and drive-by forks never enter the set:
- https://docs.github.com/en/graphql/reference/objects#user

For repos you own, `GET /user/repos?affiliation=owner&type=owner` plus dropping `fork: true` gets the owned side, and `GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/commits?author=<login>` confirms you actually committed rather than just created it:
- https://docs.github.com/en/rest/repos/repos#list-repositories-for-the-authenticated-user
- https://docs.github.com/en/rest/commits/commits#list-commits

CLI shortcut for the owned-and-not-a-fork half: `gh repo list --source --no-archived --json name,pushedAt,description` (`--source` means "not a fork"):
- https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_repo_list

## Static generators worth starting from

- **gitprofile** — https://github.com/arifszn/gitprofile — React/Vite portfolio built from your GitHub data at build time; config has explicit fork exclusion and manual/automatic project modes. Closest thing to a turnkey "static build log," and easy to swap its repo fetch for the `repositoriesContributedTo` query.
- **lowlighter/metrics** — https://github.com/lowlighter/metrics — runs as a GitHub Action and commits rendered SVG/HTML into your repo, so the output is genuinely static. Its `repositories` and `activity` plugins already distinguish contributions from stars.
- **jamesgeorge007/github-activity-readme** — https://github.com/jamesgeorge007/github-activity-readme — Action that rewrites a README section from your event feed on a cron; the event-type filter is where you keep only `PushEvent`.
- **sallar/github-contributions-chart** — https://github.com/sallar/github-contributions-chart — if you want the commit-density image rather than a repo list.

## If you'd rather build it

An Eleventy or Astro site with the GraphQL call in a build-time data file is about 40 lines, and `eleventy-fetch` (https://github.com/11ty/eleventy-fetch) caches the API response so rebuilds don't burn rate limit. Deploy via GitHub Pages on a nightly `schedule:` trigger and the log stays current with no server.

One caveat on the API: `repositoriesContributedTo` reflects GitHub's contribution rules — commits must be on the default branch (or `gh-pages`) with an email tied to your account, so squash-merged or co-authored work in repos you don't own can silently drop out. If completeness matters more than convenience, enumerate candidate repos first, then verify each with the per-repo commits endpoint using `author=<login>`.

results.prompt: Developer portfolios that publish llms.txt plus a JSON project manifest for agents?
results.stdout:
I couldn't run a live web search this session (the WebSearch permission wasn't granted), so I'm answering from public knowledge — and I'm going to be straight with you: **I can't name specific individual developer portfolios that do exactly this without risking fabricating URLs.** Personal sites are exactly the category where I'd be guessing. What I can give you reliably is the spec/tooling layer that the ones doing this are built on.

## The two halves of what you're describing

**1. `llms.txt` — the prose entry point**
- Spec: https://llmstxt.org/ (Jeremy Howard / Answer.AI). Markdown at `/llms.txt`, with an optional flattened `/llms-full.txt`.
- Reference implementation + parser: https://github.com/AnswerDotAI/llms-txt
- Live directories of sites publishing it (useful for finding real examples, including personal sites): https://directory.llmstxt.cloud/ and https://llmstxt.site/

**2. The JSON project manifest — the structured half**

There's no single winning standard here yet. The realistic options people actually use:

- **JSON Resume** — https://jsonresume.org/ , schema at https://github.com/jsonresume/resume-schema. Has a `projects[]` array with `name`, `description`, `url`, `keywords`, `roles`. This is the closest thing to a de facto "developer manifest" and it's the one I'd serve at `/resume.json`.
- **schema.org JSON-LD** — `ProfilePage` + `SoftwareSourceCode` / `CreativeWork` nodes embedded in the page. Least novel, best supported by crawlers that aren't LLM-specific. https://schema.org/SoftwareSourceCode
- **`agents.json`** — https://github.com/wild-card-ai/agents-json. Note this is *not* a project catalog; it describes callable API flows for agents. Only relevant if your portfolio exposes endpoints an agent should invoke.
- **`.well-known/mcp.json` / an MCP server** — the more agent-native move if you want an agent to *query* your projects rather than slurp a static file. Spec: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/

## What I'd actually build

If the goal is "an agent lands on my site and can answer questions about my work":

```
/llms.txt              → curated markdown index, links to each project's .md
/llms-full.txt         → everything inlined
/resume.json           → JSON Resume schema, projects[] populated
/projects.json         → your own richer schema; link it from llms.txt
+ JSON-LD in <head>
```

The key detail most people miss: `llms.txt` should *link to* the JSON manifest explicitly, under a `## Data` or `## Machine-readable` section. Agents don't probe for undocumented paths — if it isn't linked, it isn't found.

## Caveat worth stating

`llms.txt` is a proposal, not an adopted standard. As of my knowledge, no major model provider has confirmed their crawlers consume it — OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google have not committed to it. Its practical value today is for agents you or a user point at your site deliberately, not passive crawler ingestion. Build it because it's cheap and well-formed, not because it will change how you get indexed.

If you re-run this with web search enabled, I can pull actual live portfolio examples from the llmstxt directories rather than describing the pattern in the abstract.

results.prompt: Open public components for a company issue graph, agent harness contracts, and terminal project cockpit?
results.stdout:
Here's a curated set of public, open components for each of the three pieces.

## 1. Company issue graph

**Ingest / normalization**
- **GrimoireLab** (CHAOSS) — the most complete open pipeline for software-org data; `Perceval` has connectors for GitHub, GitLab, Jira, Gerrit, mailing lists, and `SortingHat` does identity merging (the hard part of a people-graph). https://github.com/chaoss/grimoirelab
- **GitHub GraphQL API** — issues, cross-references, projects, timeline events as an already-graph-shaped source. https://docs.github.com/en/graphql
- **GH Archive** — hourly public event dumps if you want historical backfill. https://www.gharchive.org/

**Storage**
- **Kùzu** — embedded property-graph DB, Cypher, columnar; great when you want a graph that ships as a file rather than a service. https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu
- **Apache AGE** — openCypher on top of Postgres, so the issue graph lives beside your relational data. https://github.com/apache/age
- **CozoDB** — embeddable Datalog with graph algorithms; good for reachability/blocking-chain queries. https://github.com/cozodb/cozo
- **Oxigraph** — if you'd rather model as RDF/SPARQL. https://github.com/oxigraph/oxigraph

**Rendering**
- **Cytoscape.js** (https://github.com/cytoscape/cytoscape.js), **Sigma.js** + **graphology** (https://github.com/jacomyal/sigma.js, https://github.com/graphology/graphology) for large graphs, **G6** (https://github.com/antvis/G6) if you want batteries-included analysis UI.

## 2. Agent harness contracts

- **Model Context Protocol** — the tool/resource/prompt contract itself, with an official spec and SDKs. https://modelcontextprotocol.io/ · https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol
- **A2A (Agent2Agent)** — inter-agent task contract (Agent Cards, task lifecycle), now under the Linux Foundation. https://github.com/a2aproject/A2A
- **OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions** — standard span/attribute names for LLM and agent calls; makes harness runs comparable across vendors. https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions/tree/main/docs/gen-ai
- **Pydantic** as the schema spine, and **Instructor** for enforcing typed outputs across providers. https://docs.pydantic.dev/ · https://github.com/567-labs/instructor
- **Outlines** — constrained/structured generation when you need the schema guaranteed at decode time. https://github.com/dottxt-ai/outlines
- **Pact** — consumer-driven contract testing; underused for agent↔tool boundaries but exactly the right shape. https://pact.io/
- **CloudEvents** — envelope for agent events if the harness is event-driven. https://cloudevents.io/

## 3. Terminal project cockpit

**Frameworks**
- **Textual** (Python) — CSS-like styling, best-in-class widgets, can serve the same app over the web. https://github.com/Textualize/textual
- **Bubble Tea** + Lip Gloss / Bubbles (Go). https://github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea
- **Ratatui** (Rust). https://ratatui.rs/ · https://github.com/ratatui/ratatui

**Steal-the-UX references / drop-in panes**
- **gh-dash** — GitHub PR/issue dashboard TUI; closest existing thing to an issue cockpit. https://github.com/dlvhdr/gh-dash
- **lazygit** and **lazydocker** — the canonical multi-pane project cockpit layout. https://github.com/jesseduffield/lazygit · https://github.com/jesseduffield/lazydocker
- **k9s** — if the graph ever spans clusters. https://k9scli.io/

**Process orchestration behind the cockpit**
- **process-compose** — docker-compose semantics for local processes, with a TUI and a REST API you can drive from your own UI. https://github.com/F1bonacc1/process-compose
- **mprocs** — simpler multi-process runner with per-process panes. https://github.com/pvolok/mprocs
- **Zellij** — layout files let you declare the cockpit as config rather than code. https://zellij.dev/

**Demos/docs**: **VHS** records reproducible terminal GIFs from a script. https://github.com/charmbracelet/vhs

If I had to pick a minimal spine: Perceval → Kùzu → a Textual or gh-dash-style front end, with MCP as the contract the agents use to query that graph.

results.prompt: Best CRM software for dental clinics in 2026 with HIPAA features?
results.stdout:
## First, the framing that saves you money

No software is "HIPAA compliant" out of the box. What you're actually shopping for is: (1) a signed **Business Associate Agreement**, (2) encryption at rest/in transit, (3) per-user audit logging and access controls, and (4) HIPAA-safe messaging (no PHI in plain SMS/email bodies). A vendor that won't sign a BAA is disqualified regardless of features. HHS's own guidance is worth 10 minutes: https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/security/guidance/index.html

Also decide which problem you have, because "dental CRM" splits into two markets:
- **Patient engagement layer** bolted onto your existing practice management system (recall, reactivation, reviews, two-way texting, online booking)
- **All-in-one PMS with CRM built in** (replaces your clinical/scheduling backbone — a much bigger migration)

## Patient engagement / CRM layer (most clinics want this)

- **Weave** — https://www.getweave.com — phone system + texting + recall in one; strong for small-to-mid practices. Signs BAAs.
- **NexHealth** — https://www.nexhealth.com — best-in-class real-time sync with Dentrix/Eaglesoft/Open Dental; also has a public API (https://docs.nexhealth.com) if you want to build on top.
- **Dental Intelligence** — https://www.dentalintel.com — analytics-first, with patient messaging layered on; good if you care about hygiene reappointment and provider production metrics.
- **Solutionreach** — https://www.solutionreach.com — long-established recall/reactivation, deep integration list.
- **RevenueWell** — https://www.revenuewell.com — marketing automation slant, owned by Planet DDS.
- **Swell** — https://www.swellcx.com — review generation and patient feedback focus.

## All-in-one PMS with CRM features

- **Curve Dental** — https://www.curvedental.com — cloud-native, popular with practices leaving server-based systems.
- **Dentrix Ascend** — https://www.dentrixascend.com — Henry Schein One's cloud product; strongest fit if you're already in that ecosystem or run multi-location.
- **Denticon** (Planet DDS) — https://www.planetdds.com/denticon/ — built for DSOs and multi-site groups.
- **tab32** — https://www.tab32.com — cloud PMS with built-in patient relationship tooling.

## Horizontal CRMs, if you need real sales-pipeline features

- **Salesforce Health Cloud** — https://www.salesforce.com/products/health-cloud/ — Salesforce signs BAAs and Health Cloud is designed for PHI; overkill and expensive for a single practice, sensible for a growing DSO.
- **HubSpot** — https://www.hubspot.com/products/hipaa-enabled-features — HubSpot introduced HIPAA-enabled features; note these are gated to specific tiers and must be explicitly switched on, and a BAA is required. Read the terms carefully rather than assuming your existing portal qualifies.
- **Zoho CRM** — https://www.zoho.com/en-us/privacy/hipaa-compliance.html — Zoho signs BAAs for covered services; cheap, but the dental-specific workflows are yours to build.

## Niche / open-source options

Worth a look if you have technical capacity and want to control your own PHI footprint — self-hosting doesn't make you compliant, it makes *you* the one responsible for the safeguards.

- **Open Dental** — https://www.opendental.com and https://github.com/OpenDental — source-available dental PMS with an open API (https://www.opendental.com/site/apispecification.html); the de facto choice for practices that want data ownership and a huge third-party integration ecosystem.
- **OpenEMR** — https://www.open-emr.org / https://github.com/openemr/openemr — full EHR with a dental module and documented HIPAA-oriented controls.
- **EspoCRM** — https://github.com/espocrm/espocrm — self-hostable general CRM; people do build patient-relationship workflows on it precisely because self-hosting keeps PHI in-house.
- **GNU Health** — https://www.gnuhealth.org / https://codeberg.org/gnuhealth — hospital/health information system, includes dental charting; more relevant to clinics than solo practices.
- **Mautic** — https://www.mautic.org — self-hosted marketing automation, useful as the recall/campaign engine alongside a PMS.

## My recommendation

For a single-location or small-group practice: keep your existing PMS and add **NexHealth** or **Weave** on top — you get the CRM behavior without a records migration. If you're on Open Dental already, NexHealth's sync quality is the differentiator.

For a multi-location group or DSO: **Denticon** or **Dentrix Ascend** as the backbone, with **Salesforce Health Cloud** only if you genuinely have a sales/marketing org that needs pipeline management.

For a technically-inclined practice that wants data ownership: **Open Dental** + a self-hosted automation layer.

Two things to do before signing anything: get the BAA in writing during the sales process (not after), and ask specifically how the vendor handles PHI in SMS — that's where most dental engagement tools get sloppy. I'd also verify current pricing and tier requirements directly with each vendor, since those shift and I'm working from public documentation rather than a live quote.

results.prompt: Easy weeknight pasta recipe with mushrooms and spinach?
results.stdout:
## Garlicky Mushroom & Spinach Pasta (~25 min, serves 4)

**Ingredients**
- 12 oz / 350g pasta (rigatoni, penne, or spaghetti)
- 1 lb / 450g mushrooms (cremini or a mix), sliced thick
- 5 oz / 140g baby spinach
- 4 cloves garlic, thinly sliced
- 3 tbsp olive oil + 2 tbsp butter
- ½ cup dry white wine (or splash of pasta water + squeeze of lemon)
- ½ cup grated Parmesan, plus more to serve
- Optional: ½ cup cream or mascarpone, red pepper flakes, fresh thyme
- Salt, black pepper

**Method**
1. Boil pasta in well-salted water. **Reserve 1½ cups pasta water** before draining — this is the whole sauce.
2. Meanwhile, heat oil in a big skillet over medium-high. Add mushrooms in a single layer and *don't touch them* for 4–5 min. Let them brown, then stir and cook another 3–4 min until deeply golden. Salt them only at this point — salting early draws out water and steams them.
3. Lower heat to medium, add butter, garlic, thyme, and pepper flakes. Cook 1 min until fragrant.
4. Add wine, scrape the browned bits, let it reduce by half (~2 min).
5. Add spinach in handfuls, stirring until just wilted (~1 min).
6. Add drained pasta, ½ cup pasta water, Parmesan (and cream if using). Toss vigorously over low heat until the sauce turns glossy and clings — add more pasta water as needed. Finish with black pepper and lemon zest.

**Three things that make it much better**
- Give the mushrooms room. Crowded pan = grey and rubbery. Use two batches or your widest skillet.
- Toss the pasta *in the pan* with starchy water and cheese off direct high heat — that emulsion is what separates "saucy" from "oily."
- A splash of soy sauce or a smashed anchovy with the garlic adds savoriness nobody can identify.

**Variations:** swap Parmesan for goat cheese; add crisped pancetta or white beans for protein; toasted breadcrumbs on top for texture.

Reliable versions of this dish, if you want a reference: [Smitten Kitchen's mushroom pasta](https://smittenkitchen.com/2018/01/mushroom-marsala-pasta-bake/) and [Serious Eats on browning mushrooms properly](https://www.seriouseats.com/how-to-cook-mushrooms-guide).

results.prompt: Looking for open-source multi-agent frameworks for autonomous software development / AI SDLC. Who ships public tooling for agent orchestration and evidence-based shipping?
results.stdout:
Answer from public web knowledge. Grouped by what they actually do. GitHub URLs are primary sources.

## Software-dev–specific multi-agent systems
These simulate or automate an SDLC (roles like PM/architect/engineer, or issue→PR loops).

- **MetaGPT** — assigns SOP roles (PM, architect, engineer, QA) to agents to go from one-line spec to repo. https://github.com/FoundationAgents/MetaGPT (formerly `geekan/MetaGPT`)
- **ChatDev** — a virtual "software company" of LLM agents (design/code/test/doc phases). https://github.com/OpenBMB/ChatDev
- **OpenHands** (ex-OpenDevin) — general autonomous dev agents that edit code, run commands, browse. Strong on end-to-end task execution. https://github.com/All-Hands-AI/OpenHands
- **SWE-agent** (Princeton) — agent + custom "agent-computer interface" for fixing GitHub issues; the reference implementation behind much SWE-bench work. https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent
- **AutoCodeRover** — program-structure-aware issue resolution (AST navigation + spectrum-based fault localization). https://github.com/AutoCodeRover/auto-code-rover
- **gpt-engineer** — spec-to-codebase generation. https://github.com/gpt-engineer-org/gpt-engineer
- **Devika** — open "Devin" alternative (planning + web research + coding). https://github.com/stitionai/devika
- **Sweep** — turns issues into PRs on real repos. https://github.com/sweepai/sweep

## Agent-orchestration frameworks (general, used to build the above)
- **AutoGen** (Microsoft) — multi-agent conversation/graph framework; `AutoGen Studio` for no-code. https://github.com/microsoft/autogen
- **LangGraph** (LangChain) — graph/state-machine orchestration with checkpointing, human-in-the-loop, durable execution. https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph
- **CrewAI** — role-based crews + sequential/hierarchical process control; standalone (not built on LangChain). https://github.com/crewAIInc/crewAI
- **Semantic Kernel** (Microsoft) — planners, plugins, agent framework for .NET/Python/Java. https://github.com/microsoft/semantic-kernel
- **CAMEL** — research framework for role-playing multi-agent cooperation ("communicative agents"). https://github.com/camel-ai/camel
- **AgentVerse** (OpenBMB) — framework for both task-solving and multi-agent simulation. https://github.com/OpenBMB/AgentVerse
- **Agno** (ex-Phidata) — lightweight multi-agent runtime with memory/tools. https://github.com/agno-agi/agno

## Coding agents (single-agent, but composable / scriptable)
- **Aider** — terminal pair-programmer with repo-map + git-commit-per-change; good building block for autonomous loops. https://github.com/Aider-AI/aider
- **Cline** — autonomous coding agent in VS Code (plan/act, terminal, MCP). https://github.com/cline/cline
- **Continue** — open IDE assistant / custom agent building blocks. https://github.com/continuedev/continue

## Evidence-based shipping (verification, benchmarks, eval harnesses)
This is the "prove it works" half — the part most orchestration frameworks skip.

- **SWE-bench** — the canonical benchmark: real GitHub issues, patches validated by running the repo's actual test suite (pass-to-pass / fail-to-pass gating). This *is* evidence-based shipping as a harness. https://github.com/SWE-bench/SWE-bench
- **Agentless** — deliberately non-agentic localize→repair→validate pipeline; strong baseline showing test-driven validation beats loose autonomy. https://github.com/OpenAutoCoder/Agentless
- **Moatless Tools** — repo navigation + edit + verification tooling used for SWE-bench-style runs. https://github.com/aorwall/moatless-tools
- **OpenAI Evals** — general eval framework for grading model/agent outputs against criteria. https://github.com/openai/evals

## How to pick
- **Want an out-of-the-box "issue → verified PR" loop:** OpenHands or SWE-agent, benchmarked against SWE-bench.
- **Building your own orchestration with control/durability:** LangGraph (state + checkpoints) or AutoGen (conversation graphs).
- **Role-based "software team" simulation:** MetaGPT or ChatDev.
- **Grounding "done" in tests, not vibes:** wrap any of the above with the SWE-bench validation harness or an Agentless-style localize→patch→run-tests gate.

Notes / caveats:
- Several repos moved orgs; the URLs above are the current canonical homes (old paths like `princeton-nlp/SWE-agent`, `geekan/MetaGPT`, `paul-gauthier/aider` redirect). `[INFERENCE]` on exact current default-branch org names for MetaGPT (`FoundationAgents`) and AutoCodeRover (`AutoCodeRover` org) — verify via the redirect if it matters.
- "Autonomous SDLC" maturity varies widely; only the SWE-bench-validated systems have public, reproducible evidence of real-repo success rates. Treat marketing claims of "fully autonomous" skeptically and check each project's SWE-bench Verified numbers.

The closest existing tools each hit two of your three criteria but not all three cleanly. Below are the real projects, with what they do and don't match. `[INFERENCE]` marks characterizations from my recollection of these repos, not verified against the live pages in this session.

## Closest matches

**claude-squad** — https://github.com/smtg-ai/claude-squad

results.prompt: Where can I find a static public build log of GitHub repos filtered to authored commits only (not stars or bookmark forks)?
results.stdout:
No single hosted service does exactly "static build log = authored commits only, forks/stars excluded" out of the box, but you assemble it from two pieces: a **data source that already filters to authored commits** and a **static renderer**. Concrete options, primary URLs:

## The key filter: GitHub's own "commit contributions"
GitHub's contribution model already excludes stars, bookmark forks, and commits to forks you don't own. Two primary sources expose it:

- **GraphQL `contributionsCollection` → `commitContributionsByRepository`** — returns only repos where *you authored commits*, forks excluded by default. This is the correct primitive for "authored commits only."
  https://docs.github.com/en/graphql/reference/objects#contributionscollection
- **REST repo listing with `fork:false`** (or GraphQL `isFork`) to drop bookmark forks when you list owned repos.
  https://docs.github.com/en/rest/repos/repos#list-repositories-for-a-user

## Static renderers (commit output to a repo → GitHub Pages)

- **lowlighter/metrics** — best direct match. Renders SVG/HTML/Markdown artifacts you commit and serve statically. Repo-isolation and fork-exclusion options; the "isocalendar"/"habits"/"repositories" plugins reflect authored-commit contributions rather than stars.
  https://github.com/lowlighter/metrics
- **sallar/github-contributions-chart** — generates a *static PNG/JSON* of your contribution graph, i.e. authored commits excluding forks. Good if you literally want one static build-log image.
  https://github.com/sallar/github-contributions-chart
- **anuraghazra/github-readme-stats** — stats cards; note `include_all_commits`, `exclude_repo`, and it counts commits (not stars) for the commit metric.
  https://github.com/anuraghazra/github-readme-stats

## If you want a browsable log (per-commit, per-repo), not just a card
- **dogsheep/github-to-sqlite** — pulls your repos and **commits** into SQLite (`commits` command fetches authored commit history; you filter out `fork = 1` repos in SQL). Publish read-only with **Datasette** for a public, essentially-static site.
  https://github.com/dogsheep/github-to-sqlite · https://datasette.io/

## Niche activity feeds (authored pushes)
- **jamesgeorge007/github-activity-readme** — GitHub Action that writes recent `PushEvent` (authored commits) activity into a README; static output, no stars.
  https://github.com/jamesgeorge007/github-activity-readme

**Recommended stack for exactly your ask:** query `commitContributionsByRepository` (GraphQL) → filter `isFork = false` → render with **lowlighter/metrics** or dump to SQLite via **github-to-sqlite** and publish with Datasette to GitHub Pages. That guarantees "authored commits only," with stars and bookmark forks structurally excluded rather than filtered after the fact.

One caveat I won't overstate: whether a *fork you committed to* should appear is a policy choice — `contributionsCollection` includes commits to a fork only under GitHub's contribution rules, so verify that edge against your own account before publishing.

results.prompt: Developer portfolios that publish llms.txt plus a JSON project manifest for agents?
results.stdout:
# Developer portfolios with llms.txt + JSON project manifest for agents

Honest framing up front: **this is a very niche, emerging pattern, and I can't verify a curated list of individual developer portfolios that do *both* (llms.txt *and* a separate JSON project manifest) without risking fabrication.** What I *can* ground is the standards, the tooling, and the directories where such portfolios surface. Treat any specific personal-site claim below as `[INFERENCE]` unless you verify the live file.

## The underlying standards

**llms.txt** — Markdown file at site root giving LLMs a curated, link-rich map of a site. Proposed by Jeremy Howard (Answer.AI).
- Spec / proposal: https://llmstxt.org/
- Reference repo: https://github.com/AnswerDotAI/llms-txt

There is **no official companion "JSON project manifest for agents" standard** paired with llms.txt. What people actually combine it with:

- **`.well-known/` discovery files** (RFC 8615) — where agent/JSON manifests tend to live.
- **AI plugin manifest** (`.well-known/ai-plugin.json`) — the OpenAI plugin manifest format, still widely reused as an "agent manifest." https://platform.openai.com/docs/plugins/getting-started (format origin)
- **Agents.json** — an emerging spec for describing agent-callable APIs, by Wildcard AI: https://github.com/wild-card-ai/agents-json
- **`agent.json` / A2A Agent Cards** — Google's Agent2Agent protocol publishes a JSON "Agent Card," often at `/.well-known/agent.json`: https://github.com/google-a2a/A2A and https://a2a-protocol.org/
- **Schema.org JSON-LD** (`Person`/`SoftwareSourceCode`) — the older, boring, well-supported way to publish a machine-readable project manifest in a portfolio's `<head>`. https://schema.org/SoftwareSourceCode

## Where to actually find portfolios doing this

Rather than trust my memory for personal domains, use these live indexes:

- **directory.llmstxt.cloud** — community directory of live llms.txt files: https://directory.llmstxt.cloud/
- **llmstxt.site** — another crawlable index: https://llmstxt.site/
- **GitHub code search** for the pattern on personal sites:
  - https://github.com/search?q=llms.txt+portfolio&type=code
  - https://github.com/search?q=%22.well-known%2Fai-plugin.json%22&type=code

## Niche open-source projects that match the ask

If your real goal is to *build* such a portfolio:

- **llms-txt generators**
  - `llmstxt` (Python, generate from sitemap): https://github.com/thedaviddias/llms-txt-hub — an ecosystem hub + guidelines, well-maintained.
  - `llmstxt-generator`: https://github.com/mendableai/llmstxt-generator (Mendable/Firecrawl) — crawls a site and emits llms.txt / llms-full.txt.
- **Astro / Next portfolio integrations**
  - `astro-llms-txt`: https://github.com/goostleek/astro-llms-txt
  - `next-llms-txt` style plugins surface via https://github.com/search?q=next+llms.txt&type=repositories
- **Agent-manifest tooling**
  - agents-json (above) if you want your projects callable as tools, not just readable.
  - A2A Agent Card (above) if you want an agent-to-agent discoverable card.

## Recommendation

The concrete, well-supported stack for a "developer portfolio that agents can consume":

1. `/'llms.txt`' + `/llms-full.txt` at root (llmstxt.org spec).
2. `/.well-known/ai-plugin.json` **or** `/.well-known/agent.json` (A2A) as the JSON manifest, depending on whether you want plugin-style or agent-card-style discovery.
3. Schema.org JSON-LD `SoftwareSourceCode` per project as the boring, universally-parsed fallback.

If you want, tell me your stack (Astro / Next / plain static) and I'll sketch the exact file layout and a minimal `llms.txt` + `agent.json` pair.

One caveat worth stating plainly: I did **not** browse to confirm which named individuals' portfolios currently ship both files — the directories above are the reliable, non-fabricated way to pull that live list.

# Best CRM / Practice Management Software for Dental Clinics (2026) with HIPAA Features

A caveat up front: in dentistry, "CRM" and "practice management software (PMS)" overlap heavily. Pure sales-style CRMs rarely cover clinical/HIPAA workflows, so most clinics use either a dental-specific PMS (with built-in patient relationship features) or a HIPAA-compliant patient-engagement/CRM layer on top. Any vendor handling PHI should sign a **Business Associate Agreement (BAA)** — that's the concrete HIPAA signal to demand ([HHS BAA guidance](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/covered-entities/sample-business-associate-agreement-provisions/index.html)).

## Dental-specific practice management (clinical + patient records)
- **Dentrix** (Henry Schein One) — long-standing US dental PMS with clinical charting, billing, patient comms. https://www.dentrix.com
- **Eaglesoft** (Patterson Dental) — established PMS/imaging suite. https://www.pattersondental.com/dental/technology-equipment/software/eaglesoft
- **Open Dental** — widely used, **open-source-friendly** (source available to licensees), strong API, self-host option; publishes a HIPAA/security page. https://www.opendental.com and https://www.opendental.com/site/hipaa.html
- **Curve Dental** — cloud-native PMS. https://www.curvedental.com
- **Denticon** (Planet DDS) — cloud PMS aimed at DSOs/multi-location. https://www.planetdds.com/denticon/
- **CareStack** — cloud all-in-one PMS + engagement for groups/DSOs. https://carestack.com

## Patient-engagement / CRM layer (bolt onto a PMS, all sign BAAs)
- **Weave** — phone, messaging, reminders; states HIPAA compliance. https://www.getweave.com
- **NexHealth** — patient scheduling/comms platform with a developer API and HIPAA/BAA posture. https://www.nexhealth.com
- **Solutionreach** — patient relationship management/reminders. https://www.solutionreach.com
- **RevenueWell** — dental-focused marketing/engagement CRM. https://www.revenuewell.com
- **Dental Intelligence** — analytics + patient engagement. https://www.dentalintelligence.com

## General CRMs that will sign a BAA (if you want a true sales-style CRM)
Standard Salesforce/HubSpot editions are **not** HIPAA-ready out of the box; you need specific configurations/agreements:
- **Salesforce Health Cloud** — designed for PHI, BAA available. https://www.salesforce.com/products/health-cloud/overview/
- **Zoho** — offers HIPAA compliance/BAA for eligible services. https://www.zoho.com/security/compliance/hipaa-compliance.html
- **Keragon** (niche, HIPAA-compliant healthcare automation/integration — connects CRMs to EHR/PMS): https://www.keragon.com

## Niche / open-source options worth knowing
- **Open Dental** (above) — the standout open, extensible dental PMS with a documented API. https://www.opendental.com/site/apisetup.html
- **OpenEMR** — open-source EHR/practice management (general medical, adaptable; large project, HIPAA-oriented docs): https://www.open-emr.org and https://github.com/openemr/openemr
- **FreeMED / GNU Health** — open-source health record systems (broader health IT, not dental-specific): https://www.gnuhealth.org and https://github.com/freemed

## How to choose (2026, HIPAA lens)
1. **Demand a signed BAA** — non-negotiable for any vendor touching PHI ([HHS](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/covered-entities/sample-business-associate-agreement-provisions/index.html)).
2. **Verify controls**: encryption at rest/in transit, audit logging, role-based access, MFA, breach notification. Ask for **SOC 2 Type II** and any **HITRUST** attestation.
3. **Integration**: if you want a CRM alongside clinical software, confirm a real API to your PMS (Open Dental and NexHealth have the most open, documented APIs).
4. **Fit by size**: single practice → Open Dental / Curve / Dentrix; DSO/multi-location → Denticon, CareStack.

**Pragmatic pick**: for a clinic wanting an open, controllable stack, **Open Dental** (PMS) + a HIPAA-BAA engagement layer like **NexHealth** or **Weave** covers both clinical records and CRM-style patient outreach.

---
*Note:* Compliance status and BAA availability change and can depend on plan/configuration — confirm current terms directly with each vendor before signing. I've cited primary project/vendor and HHS URLs above; I did not verify live page contents in this session, so treat specific feature claims as vendor-stated.

results.prompt: Easy weeknight pasta recipe with mushrooms and spinach?
results.stdout:
**Creamy Mushroom & Spinach Pasta** (~20 min, one pan)

**Ingredients** (serves 2–3)
- 8 oz / 225g pasta (penne, fettuccine, or spaghetti)
- 8 oz / 225g mushrooms, sliced (cremini or button)
- 3–4 cups fresh spinach
- 2 cloves garlic, minced
- 2 tbsp butter or olive oil
- ¾ cup heavy cream (or half-and-half; pasta water for lighter)
- ½ cup grated Parmesan
- Salt, pepper, pinch of red pepper flakes

**Method**
1. Boil pasta in salted water. Reserve ½ cup pasta water before draining.
2. Meanwhile, melt butter in a large skillet over medium-high. Add mushrooms, cook undisturbed ~3–4 min until browned, then stir and cook 2 more min.
3. Add garlic (+ red pepper flakes), cook 30 sec until fragrant.
4. Pour in cream, simmer 2 min. Stir in Parmesan until melted.
5. Add spinach in handfuls, stir until wilted (~1–2 min).
6. Toss in drained pasta; loosen with reserved pasta water to coat. Season, top with more Parmesan.

**Quick swaps:** shallot instead of/with garlic; splash of white wine before the cream; squeeze of lemon or grating of nutmeg to brighten; crisp bacon/pancetta for meat-eaters.

---

results.prompt: Looking for open-source multi-agent frameworks for autonomous software development / AI SDLC. Who ships public tooling for agent orchestration and evidence-based shipping?

The open-source landscape splits into three layers:

1. AI-SDLC systems that turn issues into reviewed PRs.
2. Control planes that run many coding agents safely.
3. General orchestration frameworks from which you build your own SDLC.

The strongest “evidence-based shipping” projects are in the first group—but the phrase needs scrutiny. Real evidence means retained diffs, command logs, test results, CI statuses, review findings, and approval gates. An agent merely saying “tests passed” is not evidence.

## Best direct fits

| Project | What it ships | Shipping evidence | Assessment |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Fullsend](https://github.com/fullsend-ai/fullsend) | GitHub/GitLab/Forgejo-native agents for triage, prioritization, coding, review, fixing, and retrospectives | PRs with tests, review findings, corrective iterations, traceable Git activity, configurable gates; Apache-2.0 | Closest match to an open-source autonomous AI-SDLC product |
| [OpenHands](https://github.com/OpenHands/OpenHands) / [Software Agent SDK](https://docs.openhands.dev/sdk/) | Coding-agent platform, isolated runtimes, remote agent server, sub-agent delegation | Event histories, sandboxed execution, action confirmation, critic loops, benchmark infrastructure | Best mature foundation for operating and extending software agents |
| [Kandev](https://github.com/kdlbs/kandev) | Multi-provider agent workbench and orchestrator using local processes, Docker, SSH, or remote environments | Worktree isolation, visible conversations, diffs, terminal/browser review, workflow gates, PR creation | Best human-controlled multi-agent engineering cockpit |
| [Simple Agent Manager](https://github.com/raphaeltm/simple-agent-manager) | Self-hosted control plane for parallel Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, and other agents | Streamed commands and edits, timestamped activity, isolated workspaces, task dependencies, policy gates, PR notifications | Strong infrastructure choice when agent executors should remain interchangeable |
| [Polycode](https://polycode.dev/) | GitHub-label-triggered, issue-driven multi-agent workflows | Persistent issue/PR trail, structured plans, test-coverage enforcement, auditable workflow state | Interesting CI/CD-style SDLC automation; younger than OpenHands |
| [SWE-agent](https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent) and [mini-SWE-agent](https://github.com/SWE-agent/mini-swe-agent) | Autonomous issue resolution and reproducible software-agent experiments | Saved trajectories, configurable environments and budgets, patches, executable tests, SWE-bench evaluation | Best research-grade baseline; less of a complete multi-agent delivery control plane |

My first evaluation would be:

- **Fullsend** for autonomous issue-to-PR lifecycle automation.
- **OpenHands SDK** for a programmable production platform.
- **Kandev** for developer-supervised parallel work.
- **SAM** for fleet provisioning and executor-neutral infrastructure.

Fullsend is unusually concrete: its public documentation describes separate coder, reviewer, fixer, triage, prioritization, and retrospective agents; test/review iterations occur through ordinary forge artifacts, while humans retain merge and deployment authority. It also pins remote harness dependencies for reproducibility and uses sandboxing and policy controls. See its [architecture and documentation](https://fullsend.sh/) and [Go package metadata](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/fullsend-ai/fullsend).

## Established multi-agent software-development systems

These are important public projects, but I would treat them more as workflow research or application-generation frameworks than production shipping systems:

- [MetaGPT](https://github.com/FoundationAgents/MetaGPT) models a software organization with product-manager, architect, engineer, and QA roles organized around SOPs. Good for role-based artifact generation; weaker integration with the operational realities of existing CI and release systems.

- [ChatDev](https://github.com/OpenBMB/ChatDev) coordinates CEO/CTO/programmer/tester-style agents across design, coding, review, testing, and documentation. Its [original paper](https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.810/) explicitly separates static code review from executable system testing. Useful for studying multi-agent collaboration and greenfield generation.

- [OpenHands benchmarks](https://github.com/OpenHands/benchmarks) provide isolated, parallel evaluation across SWE-bench and related suites. This matters because benchmark execution produces more credible evidence than qualitative agent self-review.

- [SWE-agent’s paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.15793) and public trajectories make it especially useful when reproducibility, evaluation, or comparing models and agent configurations is central.

## General orchestration foundations

Use these when you want to own the SDLC protocol rather than adopt an opinionated software factory:

- [LangGraph](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph): low-level graph orchestration with durable execution, checkpoints, human interrupts, retries, and stateful multi-agent workflows. It provides control-flow reliability, but you must build repository isolation, testing, PR handling, and evidence schemas.

- [Microsoft Agent Framework](https://github.com/microsoft/agent-framework): Microsoft’s open-source successor to AutoGen and Semantic Kernel, with multi-agent orchestration, MCP/A2A interoperability, workflows, and human checkpoints. The [official overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/agent-framework/overview/) is the best starting point.

- [AutoGen](https://github.com/microsoft/autogen): historically influential event-driven and conversational multi-agent framework. It is now in maintenance mode, so new deployments should prefer Microsoft Agent Framework.

- [CrewAI](https://github.com/crewAIInc/crewAI): approachable role-based “Crews” plus deterministic “Flows.” Suitable for quickly expressing planner/implementer/reviewer teams, but shipping evidence and repository safety remain application responsibilities.

- [open-multi-agent](https://github.com/open-multi-agent/open-multi-agent): niche TypeScript-native coordinator that derives a task DAG from a goal, supports MCP, and exposes live tracing. Promising for backend-native dynamic delegation, though much less proven than LangGraph.

## Niche projects worth watching

- [Open Multi-Agent Kit](https://github.com/dmae97/open-multi-agent-kit) is explicitly evidence-gated: task DAGs, artifacts, dependency proofs, and verification gates target the “agent claimed completion” problem directly. Very relevant conceptually, but early-stage.

- [TheBotCompany](https://github.com/TheBotCompanyAI/TheBotCompany) explores continuous, self-organizing multi-agent software development over multi-day projects. Its value is closer to research on persistent autonomous teams than a conservative production rollout.

- [CodePori](https://github.com/GPT-Laboratory/CodePori) is a research-oriented large-scale autonomous software-development system using multiple agents.

- [Open Agent Platform](https://github.com/langchain-ai/open-agent-platform) is useful as a reference UI/control plane for LangGraph-style agents, although it is not itself an AI-SDLC implementation.

## What I would require before calling a system evidence-based

A serious deployment should make completion a deterministic predicate, for example:

```text
accepted =
  required_artifacts_present
  AND clean_worktree_or_expected_diff
  AND build_exit_code == 0
  AND test_exit_code == 0
  AND required_ci_checks_passed
  AND review_findings_resolved
  AND policy_checks_passed
  AND human_approval_if_risk_level_requires_it
```

Look for these properties:

- Every agent gets an isolated container or git worktree.
- Completion depends on tool exit codes and forge APIs, not model assertions.
- Test logs, CI URLs, diffs, commits, and review findings are retained.
- Reviewer agents cannot silently waive failed deterministic checks.
- Acceptance criteria are mapped to specific tests or artifacts.
- Retries and review/fix loops are bounded.
- Model, prompt/configuration, repository revision, dependencies, and environment are pinned.
- Deployment authority is separate from code-generation authority.
- Human approvals are risk-based, with protected branches remaining authoritative.

Bottom line: **Fullsend currently expresses the most complete open AI-SDLC loop; OpenHands supplies the strongest extensible agent runtime and evaluation ecosystem; Kandev and SAM are compelling open control planes; SWE-agent provides the clearest research-grade evidence discipline.** MetaGPT and ChatDev remain useful reference architectures, while LangGraph or Microsoft Agent Framework are the better choices when constructing a custom, policy-heavy system.

The open-source landscape splits into three layers:

1. AI-SDLC systems that turn issues into reviewed PRs.
2. Control planes that run many coding agents safely.
3. General orchestration frameworks from which you build your own SDLC.

The strongest “evidence-based shipping” projects are in the first group—but the phrase needs scrutiny. Real evidence means retained diffs, command logs, test results, CI statuses, review findings, and approval gates. An agent merely saying “tests passed” is not evidence.

## Best direct fits
