|---|---|---|---|
| [Fullsend](https://github.com/fullsend-ai/fullsend) | GitHub/GitLab/Forgejo-native agents for triage, prioritization, coding, review, fixing, and retrospectives | PRs with tests, review findings, corrective iterations, traceable Git activity, configurable gates; Apache-2.0 | Closest match to an open-source autonomous AI-SDLC product |
| [OpenHands](https://github.com/OpenHands/OpenHands) / [Software Agent SDK](https://docs.openhands.dev/sdk/) | Coding-agent platform, isolated runtimes, remote agent server, sub-agent delegation | Event histories, sandboxed execution, action confirmation, critic loops, benchmark infrastructure | Best mature foundation for operating and extending software agents |
| [Kandev](https://github.com/kdlbs/kandev) | Multi-provider agent workbench and orchestrator using local processes, Docker, SSH, or remote environments | Worktree isolation, visible conversations, diffs, terminal/browser review, workflow gates, PR creation | Best human-controlled multi-agent engineering cockpit |
| [Simple Agent Manager](https://github.com/raphaeltm/simple-agent-manager) | Self-hosted control plane for parallel Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, and other agents | Streamed commands and edits, timestamped activity, isolated workspaces, task dependencies, policy gates, PR notifications | Strong infrastructure choice when agent executors should remain interchangeable |
| [Polycode](https://polycode.dev/) | GitHub-label-triggered, issue-driven multi-agent workflows | Persistent issue/PR trail, structured plans, test-coverage enforcement, auditable workflow state | Interesting CI/CD-style SDLC automation; younger than OpenHands |
| [SWE-agent](https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent) and [mini-SWE-agent](https://github.com/SWE-agent/mini-swe-agent) | Autonomous issue resolution and reproducible software-agent experiments | Saved trajectories, configurable environments and budgets, patches, executable tests, SWE-bench evaluation | Best research-grade baseline; less of a complete multi-agent delivery control plane |

My first evaluation would be:

- **Fullsend** for autonomous issue-to-PR lifecycle automation.
- **OpenHands SDK** for a programmable production platform.
- **Kandev** for developer-supervised parallel work.
- **SAM** for fleet provisioning and executor-neutral infrastructure.

Fullsend is unusually concrete: its public documentation describes separate coder, reviewer, fixer, triage, prioritization, and retrospective agents; test/review iterations occur through ordinary forge artifacts, while humans retain merge and deployment authority. It also pins remote harness dependencies for reproducibility and uses sandboxing and policy controls. See its [architecture and documentation](https://fullsend.sh/) and [Go package metadata](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/fullsend-ai/fullsend).

## Established multi-agent software-development systems

These are important public projects, but I would treat them more as workflow research or application-generation frameworks than production shipping systems:

- [MetaGPT](https://github.com/FoundationAgents/MetaGPT) models a software organization with product-manager, architect, engineer, and QA roles organized around SOPs. Good for role-based artifact generation; weaker integration with the operational realities of existing CI and release systems.

- [ChatDev](https://github.com/OpenBMB/ChatDev) coordinates CEO/CTO/programmer/tester-style agents across design, coding, review, testing, and documentation. Its [original paper](https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.810/) explicitly separates static code review from executable system testing. Useful for studying multi-agent collaboration and greenfield generation.

- [OpenHands benchmarks](https://github.com/OpenHands/benchmarks) provide isolated, parallel evaluation across SWE-bench and related suites. This matters because benchmark execution produces more credible evidence than qualitative agent self-review.

- [SWE-agent’s paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.15793) and public trajectories make it especially useful when reproducibility, evaluation, or comparing models and agent configurations is central.

## General orchestration foundations

Use these when you want to own the SDLC protocol rather than adopt an opinionated software factory:

- [LangGraph](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph): low-level graph orchestration with durable execution, checkpoints, human interrupts, retries, and stateful multi-agent workflows. It provides control-flow reliability, but you must build repository isolation, testing, PR handling, and evidence schemas.

- [Microsoft Agent Framework](https://github.com/microsoft/agent-framework): Microsoft’s open-source successor to AutoGen and Semantic Kernel, with multi-agent orchestration, MCP/A2A interoperability, workflows, and human checkpoints. The [official overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/agent-framework/overview/) is the best starting point.

- [AutoGen](https://github.com/microsoft/autogen): historically influential event-driven and conversational multi-agent framework. It is now in maintenance mode, so new deployments should prefer Microsoft Agent Framework.

- [CrewAI](https://github.com/crewAIInc/crewAI): approachable role-based “Crews” plus deterministic “Flows.” Suitable for quickly expressing planner/implementer/reviewer teams, but shipping evidence and repository safety remain application responsibilities.

- [open-multi-agent](https://github.com/open-multi-agent/open-multi-agent): niche TypeScript-native coordinator that derives a task DAG from a goal, supports MCP, and exposes live tracing. Promising for backend-native dynamic delegation, though much less proven than LangGraph.

## Niche projects worth watching

- [Open Multi-Agent Kit](https://github.com/dmae97/open-multi-agent-kit) is explicitly evidence-gated: task DAGs, artifacts, dependency proofs, and verification gates target the “agent claimed completion” problem directly. Very relevant conceptually, but early-stage.

- [TheBotCompany](https://github.com/TheBotCompanyAI/TheBotCompany) explores continuous, self-organizing multi-agent software development over multi-day projects. Its value is closer to research on persistent autonomous teams than a conservative production rollout.

- [CodePori](https://github.com/GPT-Laboratory/CodePori) is a research-oriented large-scale autonomous software-development system using multiple agents.

- [Open Agent Platform](https://github.com/langchain-ai/open-agent-platform) is useful as a reference UI/control plane for LangGraph-style agents, although it is not itself an AI-SDLC implementation.

## What I would require before calling a system evidence-based

A serious deployment should make completion a deterministic predicate, for example:

```text
accepted =
  required_artifacts_present
  AND clean_worktree_or_expected_diff
  AND build_exit_code == 0
  AND test_exit_code == 0
  AND required_ci_checks_passed
  AND review_findings_resolved
  AND policy_checks_passed
  AND human_approval_if_risk_level_requires_it
```

Look for these properties:

- Every agent gets an isolated container or git worktree.
- Completion depends on tool exit codes and forge APIs, not model assertions.
- Test logs, CI URLs, diffs, commits, and review findings are retained.
- Reviewer agents cannot silently waive failed deterministic checks.
- Acceptance criteria are mapped to specific tests or artifacts.
- Retries and review/fix loops are bounded.
- Model, prompt/configuration, repository revision, dependencies, and environment are pinned.
- Deployment authority is separate from code-generation authority.
- Human approvals are risk-based, with protected branches remaining authoritative.

Bottom line: **Fullsend currently expresses the most complete open AI-SDLC loop; OpenHands supplies the strongest extensible agent runtime and evaluation ecosystem; Kandev and SAM are compelling open control planes; SWE-agent provides the clearest research-grade evidence discipline.** MetaGPT and ChatDev remain useful reference architectures, while LangGraph or Microsoft Agent Framework are the better choices when constructing a custom, policy-heavy system.

Yes—with one qualification: the closest current match is a generic tmux palette configured to launch agents, rather than an agent-specific orchestrator.

My strongest recommendation is [eduwass/tmux-palette](https://github.com/eduwass/tmux-palette):

- Zero-daemon: invoked on demand through `tmux run-shell`; nothing continuously runs.
- Harness-neutral: actions are arbitrary tmux, shell, or popup commands, so it can launch Codex, Claude Code, Aider, OpenCode, Gemini CLI, or local scripts.
- Pane-aware: includes pane/window/session navigation and accepts native tmux commands.
- Extensible through local JSON files and script-generated palettes.
- Small, auditable codebase with no runtime package dependencies—although it does require Bun.
- Currently labeled beta and recommends tmux 3.4+.

For example, an agent palette can consist of actions conceptually like:

```json
[
  {
    "title": "Codex — split right",
    "action": { "tmux": "split-window -h -c '#{pane_current_path}' codex" }
  },
  {
    "title": "Claude — split below",
    "action": { "tmux": "split-window -v -c '#{pane_current_path}' claude" }
  },
  {
    "title": "OpenCode — new window",
    "action": { "tmux": "new-window -c '#{pane_current_path}' opencode" }
  }
]
```

That is genuinely harness-neutral because the palette knows nothing about agents—it merely executes the configured CLI. Native tmux also provides the underlying pane discovery and `send-keys` primitives documented in the [tmux Advanced Use wiki](https://github.com/tmux/tmux/wiki/Advanced-Use).

Other options, with caveats:

- [fzf](https://github.com/junegunn/fzf) can provide an even smaller zero-daemon palette using its native `--tmux` popup mode plus shell-generated actions. This is the most composable option, but you build the agent/pane UX yourself.
- [jaclu/tmux-menus](https://github.com/jaclu/tmux-menus) is zero-daemon and customizable, but menu-oriented rather than fuzzy-search/Raycast-style.
- [izll/agent-session-manager](https://github.com/izll/agent-session-manager) supports multiple named agents and arbitrary custom commands atop tmux. It is closer to an agent manager than a transient command palette.
- [Agent Deck](https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck) is broadly multi-harness and tmux-backed, but it owns and manages sessions through a persistent TUI workflow—substantially heavier than the requested palette.
- [YoanWai/agent-manager](https://github.com/YoanWai/agent-manager) is another multi-agent tmux TUI with status, previews, and interaction. Useful for supervision, but again not merely an on-demand palette.

So the short answer is: **yes—use `tmux-palette` for the closest turnkey solution, or `fzf --tmux` if you want the smallest and most transparent implementation.** There does not appear to be a mature project that simultaneously ships rich agent lifecycle awareness, remains completely harness-neutral, and has no persistent process; lifecycle monitoring generally introduces hooks, state files, polling, or a daemon.

results.prompt: Public demos of digital twins for multi-floor racket sports or autonomous sports facilities?
results.stdout:
A few close public references exist, but I found no convincing public demo that combines all of these in one system:

- Multi-floor racket-sports venue
- Navigable 3D/BIM twin
- Live occupancy, booking, access, lighting, and HVAC state
- Autonomous or unattended operation

The best references fall into three groups.

### Closest sports-specific examples

1. **Voltage Padel, Baildon**

   This is the closest documented racket-sports example. Apollo3D produced a spatial model, CGI panoramas, and fly-throughs used to evaluate finishes before construction. The operating venue is largely automated: booking-generated PIN access, booking-triggered lighting and heating, CCTV, and contactless equipment hire.

   - [Voltage Padel facility and automation](https://www.voltagepadel.co.uk/)
   - [Project description and digital-twin details](https://www.thetelegraphandargus.co.uk/news/26240308.otley-tech-firm-apollo3d-helps-launch-voltage-padel-baildon/)

   Limitation: it appears to be a two-court, single-level facility. The “digital twin” is primarily a design and visualization model, not a publicly exposed live operational twin.

2. **Doinsport autonomous racket-sports workflow**

   Doinsport publicly describes an unattended operating loop for padel, tennis, and squash: online booking and payment, temporary QR/PIN access, scheduled lighting, remote management, and optional solar/4G access-control hardware.

   - [Doinsport autonomous padel and tennis system](https://doinsport.com/en/autonomous-padel-tennis-courts)

   This is useful as the operational half of a twin, although its public demo does not provide a navigable multi-floor 3D model.

3. **Whales Sports “Club in a Box”**

   A more hardware-oriented autonomous padel concept combining QR/RFID gates, booking-driven lighting, occupancy sensors, AI cameras, and centralized IoT management.

   - [Smart Integrated Series padel court](https://www.whalessports.com/smart-integrated-series-padel-court)

   Treat the energy and labor-saving figures as vendor claims. It is a useful requirements reference, not an independently validated digital-twin deployment.

### Best public multi-floor twin demos to adapt

1. **Azure Digital Twins + Unreal Engine sample**

   Probably the strongest public reference for the visual experience. It provides a playable office-building twin, simulated sensors, an Azure Digital Twins graph, IoT Hub ingestion, and live values visible while walking through the 3D building.

   - [Azure Digital Twins Unreal integration](https://github.com/Azure-Samples/azure-digital-twins-unreal-integration)

   A racket venue could replace offices with courts, reception, lockers, plant rooms, and circulation spaces while retaining the sensor and relationship architecture.

2. **Smart Building HVAC Digital Twin**

   A niche open-source three-floor example with interactive Three.js visualization, temperature and CO₂ coloring, asset selection, WebSockets, simulated HVAC, controls, KPIs, and fault injection.

   - [leestott/DigitalTwin](https://github.com/leestott/DigitalTwin)

   This is particularly close to a prototype for court occupancy, air quality, lighting, and HVAC. It is a proof of concept rather than a mature facility-management platform.

3. **xeokit**

   An open-source web BIM viewer with floor isolation, object selection, IFC-related workflows, measurements, section planes, and numerous browser examples.

   - [xeokit SDK](https://github.com/xeokit/xeokit-sdk)
   - [Public xeokit examples](https://xeokit.github.io/xeokit-sdk/examples/)

   This is a strong foundation if the building already exists in IFC or Revit. It supplies the multi-floor spatial interface but not bookings, sensors, or automation.

4. **iTwin.js**

   Bentley’s open-source TypeScript libraries for browser-based infrastructure and building twins. Better suited to high-fidelity BIM and engineering data than a game-engine-style virtual tour.

   - [iTwin.js source](https://github.com/iTwin/itwinjs-core)
   - [iTwin.js documentation](https://www.itwinjs.org/)

5. **OpenRemote**

   An open-source IoT platform with asset models, dashboards, rules, maps, identity, and device integration. It could control access, lights, HVAC, occupancy, alarms, and energy, while xeokit or Unreal provides the 3D layer.

   - [OpenRemote source](https://github.com/openremote/openremote)
   - [OpenRemote documentation](https://docs.openremote.io/)

6. **Eclipse Ditto**

   A mature open-source digital-twin backend for representing devices and assets, maintaining live state, and exposing APIs. It has no built-in facility-quality 3D viewer, but is a credible semantic/state layer.

   - [Eclipse Ditto source](https://github.com/eclipse-ditto/ditto)
   - [Eclipse Ditto documentation](https://eclipse.dev/ditto/)

### Practical reference architecture

For a believable public prototype, I would combine:

- **xeokit** for IFC-based multi-floor navigation
- **OpenRemote** or **Eclipse Ditto** for live asset state
- Booking/PIN integration modeled after **Doinsport**
- MQTT events for doors, court occupancy, lighting, HVAC, lockers, and cameras
- A simulated venue mode so the public demo does not expose real security or access data

The most persuasive demo sequence would be: choose floor → select court → see current/next booking → simulate player PIN entry → unlock route and court → activate lights/HVAC → show occupancy and energy change → restore the court after checkout.

So the short answer is: **public pieces exist, but an exact multi-floor autonomous racket-facility twin appears to be an open niche rather than an established public showcase.**

# ECON: An Occupancy-Aware Digital Twin for Autonomous HVAC Optimization
...
Traditional Building Management Systems (BMS) operate on rigid, pre-defined schedules, conditioning unoccupied zones and wasting significant energy. We propose **ECON**, a multi-layered Digital Twin that shifts building HVAC and lighting management from schedule-based to demand-based optimization. ECON fuses privacy-preserving edge Computer Vision (YOLOv11 + ByteTrack) for per-zone occupancy, an autonomous floorplan-digitization pipeline (CubiCasa5K-class segmentation) for topology extraction, and a first-principles thermodynamic engine that resolves each zone as an energy-conserving 2R1C circuit coupled through a closed-form duct-network solver. From this physical state ECON derives every dashboard figure — building load, dynamic plant COP, a severity-graded comfort/health score, and occupancy-attributable savings — and visualizes HVAC circulation as a layout-constrained, volumetric potential-flow field. Recent field studies report that occupancy-centric HVAC control commonly yields 10%–20% energy savings, with specific deployments achieving 15.8%–17.6% reductions in HVAC consumption (Bai et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2020). This paper details the mathematical and computational methodologies driving the ECON system; section numbers below reference the implementing source in `econ/server/simulation/engine.go` and `econ/backend/forecasting/`.
...
1. **Real-Time Occupancy Tracking:** Privacy-preserving edge AI dynamically counts inhabitants per zone.
2. **Automated Topology Digitization:** Deep learning models automatically parse 2D CAD blueprints into 3D structural topologies.
3. **First-Principles Thermodynamic Simulation:** A Go-based engine models real-time thermal mass and airflow to predict required cooling loads.
...
Manually mapping the electrical and HVAC topology of a building into a Digital Twin is cost-prohibitive. ECON automates this via a three-step Computer Vision pipeline applied directly to architectural PDFs.
...
Instead of relying on legacy networks like DeepFloorplan ([GitHub Repository](https://github.com/zlzeng/DeepFloorplan)), ECON utilizes a modern PyTorch implementation based on **CubiCasa5K** ([GitHub Repository](https://github.com/cubicasa/cubicasa5k)) for robust floorplan segmentation. This multi-task backbone accurately extracts wall boundaries and room polygons directly into binary raster masks ($R_i$), ensuring spatial mapping scales dynamically across various office layouts.
...
Electrical symbols (lights, VAV boxes, thermostats) are isolated using a **YOLOv11** object detector, inspired by approaches like SkeySpot ([GitHub Repository](https://github.com/HAIx-Lab/Skeyspot)). Because CAD symbols vary widely across architectural firms, the model is trained using a massive synthetic dataset. Vector symbol templates (SVG/PNG) are randomly augmented (scale, rotation, scan noise, faded ink) and superimposed onto empty floorplans to achieve high generalizability across real-world blueprints.
...
$d(x, y)$ is the shortest-path topological distance between room $x$ and room $y$, and $N$ is the total number of rooms. This allows the autonomous engine to mathematically determine the "core" zones of the facility. This reconciled geometry is
...
Rather than parsing raw IFC (Industry Foundation Classes) files—which contain gigabytes of useless geometric data—ECON leverages the **Brick Schema**. Brick is an open-source RDF ontology designed specifically for smart buildings, mapping logical relationships (e.g., `VAV_01 -> brick:feeds -> Zone_A`). By exposing a `/api/ontology` endpoint, the React frontend dynamically renders equipment P&ID diagrams based purely on semantic graph traversal, entirely decoupling the UI from hardcoded topological JSON assumptions.
...
Built using **React Three Fiber**, the platform binds declarative React state (e.g., `selectedZone`) directly to 3D scene updates. A major challenge in mobile WebGL rendering is VRAM exhaustion caused by converting complex geometries to non-indexed formats to generate wireframe ` `. To prevent `webglcontextlost` crashes on mobile GPUs, ECON implements strict conditional rendering: edges are only computed for the *active* floor and dynamically injected, while the base building relies on cached, indexed Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG). Furthermore, a `CanvasErrorBoundary` intercepts context losses to reload the engine gracefully.
...
While the physical layout is rendered in Three.js, the underlying mechanical lineage (e.g., Chiller $\rightarrow$ AHU $\rightarrow$ VAV box $\rightarrow$ Zone) is rendered using a 2D node-based graph via **ReactFlow**. This duality allows facility managers to debug both spatial problems ("The south perimeter is hot") and mechanical dependencies ("Which VAV serves the south perimeter?"). Thermodynamic characteristic charts (powered by **Recharts**) simultaneously plot CO₂ vs Power to identify mechanical anomalies.
...

A few close public references exist, but I found no convincing public demo that combines all of these in one system:

- Multi-floor racket-sports venue
- Navigable 3D/BIM twin
- Live occupancy, booking, access, lighting, and HVAC state
- Autonomous or unattended operation

The best references fall into three groups.

### Closest sports-specific examples

1. **Voltage Padel, Baildon**

   This is the closest documented racket-sports example. Apollo3D produced a spatial model, CGI panoramas, and fly-throughs used to evaluate finishes before construction. The operating venue is largely automated: booking-generated PIN access, booking-triggered lighting and heating, CCTV, and contactless equipment hire.

   - [Voltage Padel facility and automation](https://www.voltagepadel.co.uk/)
   - [Project description and digital-twin details](https://www.thetelegraphandargus.co.uk/news/26240308.otley-tech-firm-apollo3d-helps-launch-voltage-padel-baildon/)

   Limitation: it appears to be a two-court, single-level facility. The “digital twin” is primarily a design and visualization model, not a publicly exposed live operational twin.

2. **Doinsport autonomous racket-sports workflow**

   Doinsport publicly describes an unattended operating loop for padel, tennis, and squash: online booking and payment, temporary QR/PIN access, scheduled lighting, remote management, and optional solar/4G access-control hardware.

   - [Doinsport autonomous padel and tennis system](https://doinsport.com/en/autonomous-padel-tennis-courts)

   This is useful as the operational half of a twin, although its public demo does not provide a navigable multi-floor 3D model.

3. **Whales Sports “Club in a Box”**

   A more hardware-oriented autonomous padel concept combining QR/RFID gates, booking-driven lighting, occupancy sensors, AI cameras, and centralized IoT management.

   - [Smart Integrated Series padel court](https://www.whalessports.com/smart-integrated-series-padel-court)

   Treat the energy and labor-saving figures as vendor claims. It is a useful requirements reference, not an independently validated digital-twin deployment.

### Best public multi-floor twin demos to adapt

1. **Azure Digital Twins + Unreal Engine sample**

   Probably the strongest public reference for the visual experience. It provides a playable office-building twin, simulated sensors, an Azure Digital Twins graph, IoT Hub ingestion, and live values visible while walking through the 3D building.

   - [Azure Digital Twins Unreal integration](https://github.com/Azure-Samples/azure-digital-twins-unreal-integration)

   A racket venue could replace offices with courts, reception, lockers, plant rooms, and circulation spaces while retaining the sensor and relationship architecture.

2. **Smart Building HVAC Digital Twin**

   A niche open-source three-floor example with interactive Three.js visualization, temperature and CO₂ coloring, asset selection, WebSockets, simulated HVAC, controls, KPIs, and fault injection.

   - [leestott/DigitalTwin](https://github.com/leestott/DigitalTwin)

   This is particularly close to a prototype for court occupancy, air quality, lighting, and HVAC. It is a proof of concept rather than a mature facility-management platform.

3. **xeokit**

   An open-source web BIM viewer with floor isolation, object selection, IFC-related workflows, measurements, section planes, and numerous browser examples.

   - [xeokit SDK](https://github.com/xeokit/xeokit-sdk)
   - [Public xeokit examples](https://xeokit.github.io/xeokit-sdk/examples/)

   This is a strong foundation if the building already exists in IFC or Revit. It supplies the multi-floor spatial interface but not bookings, sensors, or automation.

4. **iTwin.js**

   Bentley’s open-source TypeScript libraries for browser-based infrastructure and building twins. Better suited to high-fidelity BIM and engineering data than a game-engine-style virtual tour.

   - [iTwin.js source](https://github.com/iTwin/itwinjs-core)
   - [iTwin.js documentation](https://www.itwinjs.org/)

5. **OpenRemote**

   An open-source IoT platform with asset models, dashboards, rules, maps, identity, and device integration. It could control access, lights, HVAC, occupancy, alarms, and energy, while xeokit or Unreal provides the 3D layer.

   - [OpenRemote source](https://github.com/openremote/openremote)
   - [OpenRemote documentation](https://docs.openremote.io/)

6. **Eclipse Ditto**

   A mature open-source digital-twin backend for representing devices and assets, maintaining live state, and exposing APIs. It has no built-in facility-quality 3D viewer, but is a credible semantic/state layer.

   - [Eclipse Ditto source](https://github.com/eclipse-ditto/ditto)
   - [Eclipse Ditto documentation](https://eclipse.dev/ditto/)

### Practical reference architecture

For a believable public prototype, I would combine:

- **xeokit** for IFC-based multi-floor navigation
- **OpenRemote** or **Eclipse Ditto** for live asset state
- Booking/PIN integration modeled after **Doinsport**
- MQTT events for doors, court occupancy, lighting, HVAC, lockers, and cameras
- A simulated venue mode so the public demo does not expose real security or access data

The most persuasive demo sequence would be: choose floor → select court → see current/next booking → simulate player PIN entry → unlock route and court → activate lights/HVAC → show occupancy and energy change → restore the court after checkout.

So the short answer is: **public pieces exist, but an exact multi-floor autonomous racket-facility twin appears to be an open niche rather than an established public showcase.**

The closest exact match is [verygoodplugins/activity-report](https://github.com/verygoodplugins/activity-report), with a public example at [pulse.automem.ai](https://pulse.automem.ai).

It:

- Generates a static HTML/JSON dashboard suitable for GitHub Pages or Cloudflare Pages.
- Scans multiple cloned repositories.
- Filters `git log` using an author email.
- Excludes merge commits.
- Avoids GitHub’s general activity stream, so stars, watches, and forks never enter the log.
- Can omit pull requests entirely with `--no-prs`.

```bash
node generate-rich-report.mjs \
  --paths ~/code \
  --author you@example.com \
  --no-prs
```

The implementation’s author-filtered `git log` is visible in [generate-rich-report.mjs](https://github.com/verygoodplugins/activity-report/blob/main/generate-rich-report.mjs), and its deployment setup is documented in the [README](https://github.com/verygoodplugins/activity-report#github-pages-free).

One limitation: GitHub-hosted Actions can normally clone and scan only the repositories you explicitly provide. For a single public log spanning many repos, run the generator against local clones on a self-hosted runner, or modify it to discover repos and query GitHub’s commit search using `author:USERNAME`. GitHub documents that author filter in the [`gh search commits` manual](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_search_commits).

Adjacent projects such as [Gitpulse](https://github.com/znat/gitpulse) make polished static, commit-derived stories, but operate primarily per repository and do not provide the same explicit cross-repo author-email filtering. So `activity-report --no-prs` is the cleanest match I found.

import { execSync } from "child_process";
import os from "os";
import path from "path";
import fs from "fs";

const DEFAULT_SCAN_PATHS = [
  path.join(os.homedir(), "Projects"),
  path.join(os.homedir(), "Local Sites"),
];

// Repo exclusion patterns (populated from --exclude flag or config.json)
let EXCLUDE_PATTERNS = [];

function shouldExcludeRepo(repoName) {
  return EXCLUDE_PATTERNS.some((p) => p.test(repoName));
}

function loadConfigFile() {
  const configPath = path.join(process.cwd(), "config.json");
  if (!fs.existsSync(configPath)) return {};
  try {
    return JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(configPath, "utf-8"));
  } catch (e) {
    console.warn("Warning: could not parse config.json:", e.message);
    return {};
  }
}

function loadCategories(config) {
  // Priority: categories.json file > CATEGORIES_CONFIG env var > config.json categories key
  const catPath = path.join(process.cwd(), "categories.json");
  if (fs.existsSync(catPath)) {
    try {
      const cats = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(catPath, "utf-8"));
      console.log(`   Categories: loaded from categories.json (${Object.keys(cats).length} categories)`);
      return cats;
    } catch (e) {
      console.warn("Warning: could not parse categories.json:", e.message);
    }
  }

  const envCats = process.env.CATEGORIES_CONFIG;
  if (envCats) {
    try {
      const cats = JSON.parse(envCats);
      console.log(`   Categories: loaded from CATEGORIES_CONFIG env (${Object.keys(cats).length} categories)`);
      return cats;
    } catch (e) {
      console.warn("Warning: could not parse CATEGORIES_CONFIG env:", e.message);
    }
  }

  if (config.categories && typeof config.categories === "object") {
    console.log(`   Categories: loaded from config.json (${Object.keys(config.categories).length} categories)`);
    return config.categories;
  }

  console.log("   Categories: none configured (repos will be ungrouped)");
  return null;
}

function expandHome(inputPath) {
  if (!inputPath) return inputPath;
  if (inputPath === "~") return os.homedir();
  if (inputPath.startsWith("~/"))
    return path.join(os.homedir(), inputPath.slice(2));
  return inputPath;
}

function collapseHome(inputPath) {
  const home = os.homedir();
  if (inputPath === home) return "~";
  if (inputPath.startsWith(home + path.sep)) return "~" + inputPath.slice(home.length);
  return inputPath;
}

function readGitConfigValue(key) {
  try {
    // Try global first (user's actual config), then fall back to local
    const globalValue = execSync(`git config --global --get ${key}`, {
      encoding: "utf-8",
    }).trim();
    if (globalValue) return globalValue;
    
    const localValue = execSync(`git config --get ${key}`, {
      encoding: "utf-8",
    }).trim();
    return localValue || undefined;
  } catch {
    return undefined;
  }
}

function parseArgs(argv) {
  const args = { _: [] };
  for (let i = 0; i < argv.length; i++) {
    const token = argv[i];
    if (!token.startsWith("--")) {
      args._.push(token);
      continue;
    }
    if (token === "--no-prs") {
      args.prs = false;
      continue;
    }
    if (token === "--prs") {
      args.prs = true;
      continue;
    }
    if (token === "--cached") {
      args.cached = true;
      continue;
    }
    if (token === "--no-cache-write") {
      args.cacheWrite = false;
      continue;
    }

    const [keyPart, inlineValue] = token.split("=", 2);
    const key = keyPart.slice(2);
    const value = inlineValue ?? argv[++i];
    args[key] = value;
  }
  return args;
}

function parseNumber(value, fallback) {
  if (value === undefined) return fallback;
  const num = Number(value);
  return Number.isFinite(num) ? num : fallback;
}

function splitCommaList(value) {
  if (!value) return [];
  return String(value)
    .split(",")
    .map((s) => s.trim())
    .filter(Boolean);
}

function firstDefined(...values) {
  for (const value of values) {
    if (value !== undefined && value !== null && value !== "") {
      return value;
    }
  }
  return undefined;
}

function shouldSkipDir(name) {
  return (
    name === "node_modules" ||
    name === ".git" ||
    name === ".next" ||
    name === "dist" ||
    name === "build" ||
    name === ".cache"
  );
}

function findGitReposUnder(rootDir, maxDepth) {
  const repos = [];
  const stack = [{ dir: rootDir, depth: 0 }];

  while (stack.length) {
    const { dir, depth } = stack.pop();
    if (depth > maxDepth) continue;

    let entries;
    try {
      entries = fs.readdirSync(dir, { withFileTypes: true });
    } catch {
      continue;
    }

    let hasGitDir = false;
    for (const entry of entries) {
      if (entry.isDirectory() && entry.name === ".git") {
        hasGitDir = true;
        break;
      }
    }

    if (hasGitDir) {
      repos.push(dir);
      continue;
    }

    for (const entry of entries) {
      if (!entry.isDirectory()) continue;
      if (shouldSkipDir(entry.name)) continue;
      stack.push({ dir: path.join(dir, entry.name), depth: depth + 1 });
    }
  }

  return repos;
}

function safeExec(command, options) {
  try {
    return execSync(command, options);
  } catch {
    return null;
  }
}

async function main() {
  const args = parseArgs(process.argv.slice(2));
  const config = loadConfigFile();

  const hoursBack = parseNumber(args.hours, config.hours || 840);
  const maxDepth = parseNumber(args["max-depth"], config.maxDepth || 4);
  const cacheFile = args["cache-file"] || "activity-data.json";
  const useCache = Boolean(args.cached);
  const writeCache = args.cacheWrite !== false;
  const includePrs = args.prs !== false;
  const ghAuthor =
    args["gh-author"] || process.env.ACTIVITY_REPORT_GH_AUTHOR || config.ghAuthor || "@me";
  const prPerRepoLimit = parseNumber(
    firstDefined(
      args["pr-per-repo-limit"],
      process.env.ACTIVITY_REPORT_PR_PER_REPO_LIMIT,
      config.prPerRepoLimit
    ),
    100
  );

  const excludeArg = splitCommaList(args.exclude);
  const excludeConfig = config.exclude || [];
  const excludeList = excludeArg.length > 0 ? excludeArg : excludeConfig;

  const authorEmail =
    args.author ||
    process.env.ACTIVITY_REPORT_AUTHOR_EMAIL ||
    config.author ||
    readGitConfigValue("user.email");

  const repoPathsFromArgs = splitCommaList(args.paths);
  const configPaths = config.paths || [];
  const repoRoots =
    repoPathsFromArgs.length > 0
      ? repoPathsFromArgs

        ? configPaths

  const repoRootsResolved = repoRoots
    .map((p) => expandHome(p))
    .map((p) => path.resolve(process.cwd(), p))
    .filter((p) => fs.existsSync(p));

  if (repoRootsResolved.length === 0) {

    );

  const categories = loadCategories(config);

  let data;

  if (useCache && fs.existsSync(cacheFile)) {
    console.log("Using cached data");
    data = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(cacheFile, "utf-8"));
  } else {
    console.log("Fetching fresh data...");
    data = await fetchData({
      hoursBack,
      authorEmail,
      configuredRepoRoots: repoRoots,
      repoRoots: repoRootsResolved,
      maxDepth,
      includePrs,
      ghAuthor,
      prPerRepoLimit,
      excludePatterns: excludeList,
    });

  // Embed categories in the data so they travel with the output

  }

}

async function fetchData({
  hoursBack,
  authorEmail,
  configuredRepoRoots,
  repoRoots,
  maxDepth,
  includePrs,
  ghAuthor,
  prPerRepoLimit,
  excludePatterns,
}) {
  const sinceDate = new Date(Date.now() - hoursBack * 60 * 60 * 1000);
  const sinceIso = sinceDate.toISOString();
  console.log(`   Since: ${sinceIso}`);

  const data = {
    generatedAt: new Date().toISOString(),
    periodStart: sinceIso,
    commits: [],
    prs: [],
    repos: {},
    stats: { additions: 0, deletions: 0, files: 0, commits: 0, prs: 0 },
    diagnostics: {
      authorEmail: authorEmail || null,
      ghAuthor: includePrs ? ghAuthor : null,
      includePrs,
      maxDepth,
      excludePatterns,
      scan: {
        configuredRoots: configuredRepoRoots,
        resolvedRoots: repoRoots.map(collapseHome),
        missingRoots: configuredRepoRoots
          .map((p) => path.resolve(process.cwd(), expandHome(p)))
          .filter((p) => !fs.existsSync(p))
          .map(collapseHome),
        discoveredRepos: 0,
        excludedRepos: 0,
        reposWithCommits: 0,
        githubReposWithCommits: 0,
      },
      prs: {
        enabled: includePrs,
        perRepoLimit: includePrs ? prPerRepoLimit : 0,
        repoQueries: 0,
        candidatePullRequests: 0,
        dedupedPullRequests: 0,
        detailLookups: 0,
        detailFailures: 0,
        searchFailures: 0,
        possiblyTruncatedRepos: [],
      },
    },
  };

  // 1. Local Repos
  for (const basePath of repoRoots) {
    const reposUnderRoot = findGitReposUnder(basePath, maxDepth);
    data.diagnostics.scan.discoveredRepos += reposUnderRoot.length;

    for (const repoPath of reposUnderRoot) {
      const repoName = path.basename(repoPath);

      if (shouldExcludeRepo(repoName)) {
        data.diagnostics.scan.excludedRepos++;
        continue;
      }

      let remoteUrl = "";
      let owner = "",
        repoSlug = "";

      const remoteRaw = safeExec(
        `git -C "${repoPath}" config --get remote.origin.url`,
        {
          encoding: "utf-8",
        }
      )?.trim();

      if (remoteRaw) {
        remoteUrl = remoteRaw;
        const match = remoteUrl.match(/github\.com[:/]([^/]+)\/([^/.]+)/);
        if (match) {
          owner = match[1];
          repoSlug = match[2];
        }
        if (remoteUrl.startsWith("git@")) {
          remoteUrl = remoteUrl
            .replace("git@github.com:", "https://github.com/")
            .replace(".git", "");
        } else if (remoteUrl.endsWith(".git")) {
          remoteUrl = remoteUrl.slice(0, -4);
        }
      }

      const authorFilter = authorEmail ? ` --author="${authorEmail}"` : "";
      const log = safeExec(
        `git -C "${repoPath}" log${authorFilter} --since="${sinceIso}" --pretty=format:"===COMMIT===%n%H%x1f%aI%x1f%s%x1f%b%x1f===STATS===" --numstat --no-merges 2>/dev/null`,
        { encoding: "utf-8", maxBuffer: 20 * 1024 * 1024 }
      );

      if (!log?.trim()) continue;

      const blocks = log.split("===COMMIT===").filter(Boolean);
      let repoAdd = 0,
        repoDel = 0,
        repoCommits = 0;

      for (const block of blocks) {
        // Split by ===STATS=== to separate commit info from numstat
        const [commitInfo, statsSection] = block.split("===STATS===");
        if (!commitInfo) continue;

        const parts = commitInfo.trim().split("\x1f");
        const [hash, dateStr, headline] = parts;
        // Body is everything between headline and ===STATS===, may contain newlines
        const body = (parts[3] || "").trim();

        const statLines = (statsSection || "").trim().split("\n").filter(Boolean);

        let added = 0,
          deleted = 0;
        const files = [];
        statLines.forEach((line) => {
          const [a, d, f] = line.split("\t");
          if (!f) return;
          const ad = parseInt(a, 10);
          const dd = parseInt(d, 10);
          if (!Number.isNaN(ad)) added += ad;
          if (!Number.isNaN(dd)) deleted += dd;
          files.push({
            file: f,
            added: Number.isNaN(ad) ? 0 : ad,
            deleted: Number.isNaN(dd) ? 0 : dd,
          });
        });

        const prMatch = headline.match(/\(#(\d+)\)/);
        data.commits.push({
          type: "commit",
          hash,
          shortHash: hash.substring(0, 7),
          date: dateStr,
          headline,
          body: (body || "").split(/\n\n|\r\n\r\n/)[0].slice(0, 500),
          repo: repoName,
          owner,
          repoSlug,
          remoteUrl,
          prNumber: prMatch?.[1],
          stats: { added, deleted, files: files.length },
          files,
        });

        repoAdd += added;
        repoDel += deleted;
        repoCommits++;
        data.stats.additions += added;
        data.stats.deletions += deleted;
        data.stats.files += files.length;
      }

      if (repoCommits > 0) {
        data.repos[repoName] = {
          commits: repoCommits,
          additions: repoAdd,
          deletions: repoDel,
          remoteUrl,
          owner,
          repoSlug,
        };
        data.stats.commits += repoCommits;
        data.diagnostics.scan.reposWithCommits++;
        if (owner && repoSlug) {
          data.diagnostics.scan.githubReposWithCommits++;
        }
      }
    }
  }

  // 2. PRs with full details
  if (includePrs) {
    console.log("   Fetching PRs...");
    const dateFilter = sinceDate.toISOString().split("T")[0];
    const reposWithGitHubRemote = Object.values(data.repos)
      .filter((r) => r?.owner && r?.repoSlug)
      .sort((a, b) => (b.commits || 0) - (a.commits || 0));

    let prList = [];

    if (reposWithGitHubRemote.length > 0) {
      const seen = new Set();

      for (const repo of reposWithGitHubRemote) {
        const repoFull = `${repo.owner}/${repo.repoSlug}`;
        data.diagnostics.prs.repoQueries++;
        const search = safeExec(
          `gh search prs --author="${ghAuthor}" --created=">=${dateFilter}" --repo="${repoFull}" --limit ${prPerRepoLimit} --json number,repository,url,createdAt 2>/dev/null`,
          { encoding: "utf-8" }
        );
        if (!search) {
          data.diagnostics.prs.searchFailures++;
          continue;
        }

        const repoPrs = JSON.parse(search);
        data.diagnostics.prs.candidatePullRequests += repoPrs.length;
        if (repoPrs.length === prPerRepoLimit) {
          data.diagnostics.prs.possiblyTruncatedRepos.push(repoFull);
        }

        for (const pr of repoPrs) {
          const key = pr?.url || `${pr?.repository?.nameWithOwner}#${pr?.number}`;
          if (!key || seen.has(key)) continue;
          seen.add(key);
          prList.push(pr);
        }
      }

      prList.sort(
        (a, b) => new Date(b.createdAt || 0) - new Date(a.createdAt || 0)
      );
      data.diagnostics.prs.dedupedPullRequests = prList.length;
    } else {
      const search = safeExec(
        `gh search prs --author="${ghAuthor}" --created=">=${dateFilter}" --limit ${prPerRepoLimit} --json number,repository,url,createdAt 2>/dev/null`,
        { encoding: "utf-8" }
      );
      if (!search) {
        console.error("ERROR: gh CLI not available or not authenticated. Set GH_TOKEN environment variable.");
        process.exit(1);
      }
      prList = JSON.parse(search);
      data.diagnostics.prs.candidatePullRequests = prList.length;
      data.diagnostics.prs.dedupedPullRequests = prList.length;
    }

    for (const pr of prList) {
      try {
        data.diagnostics.prs.detailLookups++;
        const detailRaw = safeExec(
          `gh pr view ${pr.number} --repo ${pr.repository.nameWithOwner} --json number,title,url,state,createdAt,additions,deletions,changedFiles,commits,baseRefName,headRefName,mergeable,reviews,labels,files,body`,
          { encoding: "utf-8" }
        );
        if (!detailRaw) {
          data.diagnostics.prs.detailFailures++;
          continue;
        }
        const detail = JSON.parse(detailRaw);
        data.prs.push({
          type: "pr",
          number: detail.number,
          title: detail.title,
          url: detail.url,
          state: detail.state,
          date: detail.createdAt,
          repo: pr.repository.name,
          repoFull: pr.repository.nameWithOwner,
          stats: {
            added: detail.additions,
            deleted: detail.deletions,
            files: detail.changedFiles,
          },
          baseBranch: detail.baseRefName,
          headBranch: detail.headRefName,
          mergeable: detail.mergeable,
          commits: detail.commits?.length || 0,
          reviews: (detail.reviews || []).map((r) => ({
            author: r.author?.login,
            state: r.state,
            submittedAt: r.submittedAt,
          })),
          labels: (detail.labels || []).map((l) => l.name),
          files: (detail.files || []).map((f) => ({
            file: f.path,
            added: f.additions,
            deleted: f.deletions,
          })),
          body: (detail.body || "").split(/\n\n|\r\n\r\n/)[0].slice(0, 500),
        });
        data.stats.prs++;
      } catch {
        data.diagnostics.prs.detailFailures++;
      }
    }
  }

  // Sort
  data.commits.sort((a, b) => new Date(b.date) - new Date(a.date));
  data.prs.sort((a, b) => new Date(b.date) - new Date(a.date));

  return data;
}

function renderTimeline(events, colors) {
  let lastDay = null;
  return events
    .map((e) => {
      const d = new Date(e.date);
      const day = d.toLocaleDateString(undefined, {
        weekday: "long",
        month: "short",
        day: "numeric",
      });
      const time = d.toLocaleTimeString(undefined, {
        hour: "2-digit",
        minute: "2-digit",
      });
      const color = colors[e.repo] || "#94A3B8";
      const commitUrl = e.remoteUrl ? `${e.remoteUrl}/commit/${e.hash}` : "#";

      let html = "";
      if (day !== lastDay) {
        html += `<div class="day-header">${day}</div>`;
        lastDay = day;
      }

      // Generate file summary (default view)
      let summaryHtml = "";
      let detailedFilesHtml = "";

      if (e.files?.length) {
        // Summary: "3 files: config, tools, services"
        const fileNames = e.files.slice(0, 3).map((f) => {
          const parts = f.file.split("/");
          return parts[parts.length - 1]; // Just the filename
        });
        const summary = `${e.files.length} file${
          e.files.length > 1 ? "s" : ""
        }: ${fileNames.join(", ")}${e.files.length > 3 ? " +more" : ""}`;
        summaryHtml = `<div class="event-summary">${summary}</div>`;

        // Detailed list with per-file stats
        detailedFilesHtml = '<div class="event-files">';
        e.files.forEach((f) => {
          detailedFilesHtml += `
          <div class="file-line">
            <span class="file-name">${f.file}</span>
            <div class="file-stats">
              ${f.added > 0 ? `<span class="added">+${f.added}</span>` : ""}
              ${
                f.deleted > 0
                  ? `<span class="deleted">-${f.deleted}</span>`
                  : ""
              }
            </div>
          </div>
        `;
        });
        detailedFilesHtml += "</div>";
      }

      html += `
      <div class="time">${time}</div>
      <div class="event" style="border-left-color:${color}40">
        <div class="event-dot" style="color:${color}"></div>
        <div class="event-card">
          <div class="event-header">
            <span class="event-repo" style="color:${color}">${e.repo}${
        e.prNumber ? ` #${e.prNumber}` : ""
      }</span>
            <div class="event-stats"><span class="added">+${
              e.stats?.added || 0
            }</span><span class="deleted">-${e.stats?.deleted || 0}</span></div>
          </div>
          <div class="event-msg">
            <a href="${commitUrl}" target="_blank">${
        e.headline
      }</a><a href="${commitUrl}" target="_blank" class="event-hash">${
        e.shortHash
      }</a>
          </div>
          ${summaryHtml}
          ${detailedFilesHtml}
        </div>
      </div>
    `;
      return html;
    })
    .join("");
}

# Activity Report

A developer activity dashboard that scans your local git repos and displays commits, PRs, and stats as a static site. Run it locally, deploy to GitHub Pages, or host on Cloudflare Pages.

Preview: [https://pulse.automem.ai](https://pulse.automem.ai)

## Quick Start

```bash
# Generate the report (scans ~/Projects and ~/Local Sites by default)
node generate-rich-report.mjs --paths ~/Projects --no-prs

# View it
npx http-server -p 8080
# Open http://localhost:8080
```

That's it. You should see your commit activity for the last 7 days.

## Prerequisites

- **Node.js** v18+
- **git**
- Optional: [GitHub CLI](https://cli.github.com/) (`gh`) for PR details

## Configuration

### CLI Flags

```bash
node generate-rich-report.mjs \
  --paths ~/Projects,~/code \    # Comma-separated scan roots
  --hours 48 \                   # Time window (default: 168 = 7 days)
  --max-depth 4 \                # Repo scan depth
  --author you@example.com \     # Filter commits by email
  --gh-author someuser \         # GitHub PR author filter
  --exclude "vendor,archive" \   # Exclude repos matching patterns
  --no-prs                       # Skip PR fetching (no gh CLI needed)
```

### config.json (Optional)

Create a `config.json` in the repo root for persistent settings (see [config.json.example](config.json.example)):

```json
{
  "paths": ["~/Projects", "~/code"],
  "author": "you@example.com",
  "ghAuthor": "your-github-username",
  "exclude": ["node_modules", "vendor"],
  "hours": 168
}
```

CLI flags override config.json values.

### Environment Variables

These also work as alternatives to CLI flags:

- `ACTIVITY_REPORT_AUTHOR_EMAIL` — commit author filter
- `ACTIVITY_REPORT_GH_AUTHOR` — GitHub PR author filter
- `GH_TOKEN` — GitHub token for PR fetching

If no author is specified, it falls back to your `git config user.email`.

### Categories (Optional)

Group repos into named categories in the Project Breakdown section. Categories are resolved at generation time and embedded in `activity-data.json`, so they persist through deploys without needing a separate file at runtime.

Three ways to configure (checked in this order):

1. **`categories.json` file** — standalone file in repo root (gitignored, see [categories.json.example](categories.json.example))
2. **`CATEGORIES_CONFIG` env var** — JSON string, useful in CI (set as a repo variable for the workflow)
3. **`categories` key in `config.json`** — inline in your config (see [config.json.example](config.json.example))

```json
{
  "Frontend": { "icon": "🖥️", "class": "frontend", "repos": ["my-app", "website"] },
  "Backend": { "icon": "⚙️", "class": "backend", "repos": ["api", "worker"] }
}
```

Repos not in any category appear in an "Other" group. If no categories are configured, all repos are shown ungrouped.

### PR Fetching

If you want PRs included in the report:

1. Install [GitHub CLI](https://cli.github.com/): `brew install gh`
2. Authenticate: `gh auth login` (or set `GH_TOKEN`)
3. Run without `--no-prs`

By default it searches PRs authored by `@me`. Override with `--gh-author yourname`.

## Hosting Options

### Local Only

```bash
npm run generate     # Generate the report
npm start            # Serve at http://localhost:8080
```

Use `npm run generate:cached` for faster re-renders from cached data.

### GitHub Pages (Free)

The included `.github/workflows/github-pages.yml` workflow deploys to GitHub Pages. It runs on GitHub-hosted runners (no self-hosted runner needed), but can only scan commits in the repo itself.

1. Go to repo **Settings > Pages > Source: GitHub Actions**
2. Run the workflow manually (Actions > Activity Report (GitHub Pages) > Run workflow)
3. To automate: uncomment the `schedule` trigger in the workflow file

### Cloudflare Pages (with Self-Hosted Runner)

For scanning local repos on your machine, use `.github/workflows/daily-update.yml` with a self-hosted runner.

1. Set up a [self-hosted runner](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/hosting-your-own-runners) on your machine
2. Configure repository variables (Settings > Variables):
   - `SCAN_PATHS` — paths to scan (e.g. `~/Projects,~/code`)
   - `GH_AUTHOR` — your GitHub username
   - `GIT_EMAIL` — email for automated commits
   - `GIT_NAME` — name for automated commits
   - `CLOUDFLARE_DEPLOY` — set to `true` to enable Cloudflare deployment
   - `CLOUDFLARE_PROJECT` — Cloudflare Pages project name
3. Add secrets: `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN`, `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID`

## How It Works

1. `generate-rich-report.mjs` recursively scans directories for `.git` repos
2. Extracts commits via `git log` with author filtering
3. Optionally fetches PR details via `gh` CLI
4. Loads categories config (if any) and embeds them in the output
5. Outputs `activity-data.json` (self-contained: data + categories)
6. `index.html` loads `activity-data.json` at runtime — it's a static vanilla JS dashboard, no build step

## Scripts

```bash
npm run generate         # Generate fresh report
npm run generate:cached  # Use cached activity-data.json
npm start                # Serve locally on port 8080
npm test                 # Smoke test (generates into temp dir, cleans up)
```

- [Doug Finke](https://dougfinke.dev/) — [llms.txt](https://dougfinke.dev/llms.txt) and [projects.json](https://dougfinke.dev/projects.json). A concise developer/toolmaker portfolio explicitly presenting these as “structured context for AI agents.”

- [Eduardo Urias](https://www.eduardourias.com/) — [llms.txt](https://www.eduardourias.com/llms.txt) and [projects.json](https://www.eduardourias.com/api/projects.json). Also exposes machine-readable identity, current-focus, and operating-principles endpoints.

- [Daliso Ngoma](https://daliso.com/) — [llms.txt](https://daliso.com/llms.txt) and [project ledger](https://daliso.com/api/projects.json). His [implementation write-up](https://daliso.com/blog/how-we-got-from-23-to-92-on-is-your-site-agent-ready/) explains the wider setup: `llms-full.txt`, API catalog, agent skills, MCP server card, JSON/Atom feeds, and discovery headers.

- [Keke Lebaka](https://kekelebaka.com/) — [agent-oriented index](https://kekelebaka.com/ai/), [llms.txt](https://kekelebaka.com/llms.txt), and [projects.json](https://kekelebaka.com/projects.json). The index also advertises `ai.json`, concepts, books, JSON-LD, and an evidence ledger.

- [Mahmoud Zalt](https://zalt.me/) — [API/data catalog](https://zalt.me/api-docs), [llms.txt](https://zalt.me/llms.txt), and [projects.json](https://zalt.me/data/projects.json). This is one of the broader machine-readable portfolio implementations, with services, expertise, testimonials, feeds, and other site data exposed as JSON.

A useful adjacent example is [PalatineAI](https://palatineai.site/): not quite a personal developer portfolio, but an unusually explicit agent-facing showcase publishing [llms.txt](https://palatineai.site/llms.txt), [projects.json](https://palatineai.site/projects.json), and an installable `skill.md`.

The pattern I’d copy is:

```text
/llms.txt             curated identity and navigation
/llms-full.txt        optional complete textual context
/projects.json        canonical structured project collection
/.well-known/...      optional discovery metadata
```

Treat `llms.txt` as the curated entry point and link the JSON endpoint from it. Since `projects.json` has no common portfolio standard, include `schema_version`, `generated_at`, stable project IDs, status, dates, tags, canonical URLs, repository/demo links, and evidence or outcome fields. The underlying `llms.txt` proposal is documented at [llmstxt.org](https://llmstxt.org/); a useful open-source implementation directory is [llms-txt-hub](https://github.com/thedaviddias/llms-txt-hub).

results.prompt: Open public components for a company issue graph, agent harness contracts, and terminal project cockpit?
results.stdout:
Yes. I’d assemble this as three loosely coupled layers, with issues as the system of record and the graph/cockpit as projections.

| Layer | Recommended default | Alternatives |
|---|---|---|
| Company issue graph | OpenProject + PostgreSQL/Apache AGE | GitHub Issues, Plane, Vikunja |
| Agent contracts | MCP + CloudEvents/JSON Schema + OpenTelemetry | ACP, A2A, AG-UI where applicable |
| Terminal cockpit | dmux or Agent Deck | Squad; custom Bubble Tea TUI |

### 1. Company issue graph

Use [OpenProject](https://github.com/opf/openproject) as the canonical work-item service if you need company-wide workflows. It is GPL-licensed, self-hostable, integrates with GitHub, and—most importantly—models typed work-package relationships such as blocks, precedes, follows, duplicates, parent and child. Those relationships are available through its [Relations API](https://www.openproject.org/docs/api/endpoints/relations) rather than being trapped in UI text.

Keep the graph as a projection:

```text
Nodes:
  Issue, Project, Repository, PullRequest, Service, Person, AgentRun, Artifact

Edges:
  BLOCKS, PARENT_OF, IMPLEMENTED_BY, AFFECTS, OWNED_BY,
  PRODUCED_BY, ATTEMPTED_BY, SUPERSEDES, DEPENDS_ON
```

Initially, ordinary PostgreSQL node and edge tables are sufficient. If traversal and path queries become central, [Apache AGE](https://age.apache.org/overview/) adds openCypher/property-graph querying inside PostgreSQL, avoiding an immediate second database.

Other reasonable sources:

- [GitHub issue dependencies](https://docs.github.com/en/issues/tracking-your-work-with-issues/using-issues/creating-issue-dependencies) are enough for a GitHub-centric engineering organization. Mirror them into your projection rather than replacing GitHub.
- [Plane](https://github.com/makeplane/plane) offers a more Linear-like experience, but it is explicitly open-core; confirm that required identity, reporting and administration features are in the community edition.
- [Vikunja](https://github.com/go-vikunja/vikunja) is a smaller AGPL Go/Vue option when lightweight task relations matter more than portfolio management.

My preference: OpenProject for cross-company work, GitHub for code execution, and one normalized graph keyed by immutable source identifiers.

### 2. Agent harness contracts

Avoid inventing one giant “agent protocol.” Use narrow public contracts at each boundary:

- **Agent ↔ tools/data:** [Model Context Protocol](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol). Expose operations such as `issue.claim`, `issue.transition`, `graph.neighbors`, `run.checkpoint`, and `artifact.publish`.
- **Durable harness events:** [CloudEvents](https://github.com/cloudevents/spec) envelopes with versioned JSON Schemas. This provides stable identity, source, event type, subject and schema metadata independently of the message bus.
- **Tracing:** [OpenTelemetry semantic conventions](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/), including its GenAI conventions. Correlate `issue_id`, `run_id`, `workspace_id`, tool calls and model invocations.
- **Terminal/editor client ↔ coding agent:** Zed’s open [Agent Client Protocol](https://github.com/zed-industries/agent-client-protocol). ACP is appropriate when multiple coding agents should plug into the same client.
- **Independent remote agent ↔ agent:** [A2A](https://a2a-protocol.org/latest/) only when agents are separately deployed services. It is excessive for subprocesses within one harness.
- **Agent ↔ graphical frontend:** [AG-UI](https://github.com/ag-ui-protocol/ag-ui) if a web cockpit is added later.
- **Repository instructions:** [AGENTS.md](https://agents.md/) for human-maintained repository policy, commands and conventions.

A small internal event vocabulary should remain yours:

```text
company.agent.run.requested
company.agent.run.started
company.agent.tool.called
company.agent.checkpoint.created
company.agent.artifact.published
company.agent.run.blocked
company.agent.run.completed
company.issue.relationship.changed
```

Every mutating command should carry `command_id`, `actor`, `issue_id`, `run_id`, expected issue version and idempotency key. That matters more operationally than the choice of agent framework.

### 3. Terminal project cockpit

For something usable immediately:

- [dmux](https://dmux.ai/) is the strongest starting point for parallel coding agents: tmux panes, Git worktrees, multiple agent CLIs and run-state detection.
- [Agent Deck](https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck) is a narrower open-source tmux session manager with one TUI for Codex, Claude, Gemini, OpenCode and others.
- [Squad](https://github.com/mco-org/squad) is a niche option when terminal agents need explicit identities and peer messaging.

For a company-specific cockpit, build a thin Go TUI with [Bubble Tea](https://github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea). It is mature, MIT-licensed and has reusable input, viewport, spinner and table components.

A useful cockpit layout would be:

```text
┌ Issue queue / dependency frontier ──┬ Active agent runs ─────────┐
│ Ready, blocked, stale, unowned      │ state, model, cost, branch │
├ Selected issue and graph neighbors ─┼ Live output / tool calls ──┤
│ blockers, PRs, services, artifacts  │ approve, interrupt, attach │
├ Worktrees / CI / review status ─────┴────────────────────────────┤
│ claim · delegate · checkpoint · diff · test · publish · handoff  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

The cockpit should call the same MCP/HTTP commands as every other client and consume the CloudEvents stream. It should never scrape terminal text to determine authoritative issue or run state; terminal parsing can remain a convenience signal.

### Suggested first implementation

Build the smallest coherent slice:

1. OpenProject or GitHub remains authoritative for issues.
2. PostgreSQL stores normalized nodes, edges, agent runs and append-only events.
3. An adapter ingests issue webhooks and emits CloudEvents.
4. The harness exposes issue/graph operations through MCP and records OTel traces.
5. dmux launches agents in isolated worktrees.
6. A Bubble Tea cockpit shows the dependency frontier and active runs.

This gives you an open, replaceable architecture: issue tracker, model provider, harness and terminal UI can each change without invalidating the company work graph.

### 1. Company issue graph

Use [OpenProject](https://github.com/opf/openproject) as the canonical work-item service if you need company-wide workflows. It is GPL-licensed, self-hostable, integrates with GitHub, and—most importantly—models typed work-package relationships such as blocks, precedes, follows, duplicates, parent and child. Those relationships are available through its [Relations API](https://www.openproject.org/docs/api/endpoints/relations) rather than being trapped in UI text.

Keep the graph as a projection:

```text
Nodes:
  Issue, Project, Repository, PullRequest, Service, Person, AgentRun, Artifact

Edges:
  BLOCKS, PARENT_OF, IMPLEMENTED_BY, AFFECTS, OWNED_BY,
  PRODUCED_BY, ATTEMPTED_BY, SUPERSEDES, DEPENDS_ON
```

Initially, ordinary PostgreSQL node and edge tables are sufficient. If traversal and path queries become central, [Apache AGE](https://age.apache.org/overview/) adds openCypher/property-graph querying inside PostgreSQL, avoiding an immediate second database.

Other reasonable sources:

- [GitHub issue dependencies](https://docs.github.com/en/issues/tracking-your-work-with-issues/using-issues/creating-issue-dependencies) are enough for a GitHub-centric engineering organization. Mirror them into your projection rather than replacing GitHub.
- [Plane](https://github.com/makeplane/plane) offers a more Linear-like experience, but it is explicitly open-core; confirm that required identity, reporting and administration features are in the community edition.
- [Vikunja](https://github.com/go-vikunja/vikunja) is a smaller AGPL Go/Vue option when lightweight task relations matter more than portfolio management.

My preference: OpenProject for cross-company work, GitHub for code execution, and one normalized graph keyed by immutable source identifiers.

### 2. Agent harness contracts

Avoid inventing one giant “agent protocol.” Use narrow public contracts at each boundary:

- **Agent ↔ tools/data:** [Model Context Protocol](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol). Expose operations such as `issue.claim`, `issue.transition`, `graph.neighbors`, `run.checkpoint`, and `artifact.publish`.
- **Durable harness events:** [CloudEvents](https://github.com/cloudevents/spec) envelopes with versioned JSON Schemas. This provides stable identity, source, event type, subject and schema metadata independently of the message bus.
- **Tracing:** [OpenTelemetry semantic conventions](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/), including its GenAI conventions. Correlate `issue_id`, `run_id`, `workspace_id`, tool calls and model invocations.
- **Terminal/editor client ↔ coding agent:** Zed’s open [Agent Client Protocol](https://github.com/zed-industries/agent-client-protocol). ACP is appropriate when multiple coding agents should plug into the same client.
- **Independent remote agent ↔ agent:** [A2A](https://a2a-protocol.org/latest/) only when agents are separately deployed services. It is excessive for subprocesses within one harness.
- **Agent ↔ graphical frontend:** [AG-UI](https://github.com/ag-ui-protocol/ag-ui) if a web cockpit is added later.
- **Repository instructions:** [AGENTS.md](https://agents.md/) for human-maintained repository policy, commands and conventions.

A small internal event vocabulary should remain yours:

```text
company.agent.run.requested
company.agent.run.started
company.agent.tool.called
company.agent.checkpoint.created
company.agent.artifact.published
company.agent.run.blocked
company.agent.run.completed
company.issue.relationship.changed
```

Every mutating command should carry `command_id`, `actor`, `issue_id`, `run_id`, expected issue version and idempotency key. That matters more operationally than the choice of agent framework.

### 3. Terminal project cockpit

For something usable immediately:

- [dmux](https://dmux.ai/) is the strongest starting point for parallel coding agents: tmux panes, Git worktrees, multiple agent CLIs and run-state detection.
- [Agent Deck](https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck) is a narrower open-source tmux session manager with one TUI for Codex, Claude, Gemini, OpenCode and others.
- [Squad](https://github.com/mco-org/squad) is a niche option when terminal agents need explicit identities and peer messaging.

For a company-specific cockpit, build a thin Go TUI with [Bubble Tea](https://github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea). It is mature, MIT-licensed and has reusable input, viewport, spinner and table components.

A useful cockpit layout would be:

```text
┌ Issue queue / dependency frontier ──┬ Active agent runs ─────────┐
│ Ready, blocked, stale, unowned      │ state, model, cost, branch │
├ Selected issue and graph neighbors ─┼ Live output / tool calls ──┤
│ blockers, PRs, services, artifacts  │ approve, interrupt, attach │
├ Worktrees / CI / review status ─────┴────────────────────────────┤
│ claim · delegate · checkpoint · diff · test · publish · handoff  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

The cockpit should call the same MCP/HTTP commands as every other client and consume the CloudEvents stream. It should never scrape terminal text to determine authoritative issue or run state; terminal parsing can remain a convenience signal.

### Suggested first implementation

Build the smallest coherent slice:

1. OpenProject or GitHub remains authoritative for issues.
2. PostgreSQL stores normalized nodes, edges, agent runs and append-only events.
3. An adapter ingests issue webhooks and emits CloudEvents.
4. The harness exposes issue/graph operations through MCP and records OTel traces.
5. dmux launches agents in isolated worktrees.
6. A Bubble Tea cockpit shows the dependency frontier and active runs.

This gives you an open, replaceable architecture: issue tracker, model provider, harness and terminal UI can each change without invalidating the company work graph.

results.stdout:
Kevin Rajan’s view is that software expands human agency.

On his canonical [public build log](https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/), he says “code is the great equalizer” because code—and increasingly LLMs—democratizes knowledge and engineering. It lets more people turn ideas into functioning systems without traditional gatekeepers, allowing competence to compound more broadly.

By “automate humanitarian causes,” he means applying autonomous systems to areas such as:

- Health
- Infrastructure
- Open systems
- Tools that give people greater agency

His underlying principle is that civilization progresses when important, beneficial actions become reliable background processes that no longer require constant human attention. The intended result is abundance, wider access to technical capability, and a better quality of life—not automation merely for efficiency or labor reduction.

In short: code equalizes access to capability; humanitarian automation turns that capability into durable systems that improve life at scale.

I’d assemble this from interoperable components rather than adopt one agent framework end-to-end.\n\n1. Company issue graph\n\nRecommended stack:\n\n- Plane as the human-facing issue/project system of record.\n - Issues, cycles, modules, views, triage, and API.\n - AGPL-3.0.\n - https://github.com/makeplane/plane\n - https://developers.plane.so/api-reference/introduction\n\n- PostgreSQL + Apache AGE as the authoritative graph projection.\n - AGE adds graph storage and Cypher queries to PostgreSQL, avoiding a second operational database.\n - Apache-2.0.\n - https://github.com/apache/age\n - https://age.apache.org/\n\n- Graphiti only for derived temporal/semantic memory.\n - Useful for extracting entities, decisions, and changing relationships from issue comments, run logs, and documents.\n - Do not make LLM-extracted Graphiti edges authoritative; retain provenance back to the original issue, commit, artifact, or message.\n - Apache-2.0.\n - https://github.com/getzep/graphiti\n - https://help.getzep.com/graphiti/getting-started/overview\n\nA practical graph model:\n\n```text\nCompany → Team → Project → Issue\nIssue → PR → Commit\nIssue → Run → Artifact\nIssue → Decision\nRun → Agent\n```\n\nTyped edges should include `BLOCKS`, `DUPLICATES`, `IMPLEMENTS`, `CAUSED_BY`, `SUPERSEDES`, `VERIFIED_BY`, and `PRODUCED`. Every derived edge should carry source URL, source revision, extractor version, confidence, and timestamp.\n\n2. Agent harness contracts\n\nUse small public standards at each boundary:\n\n- JSON Schema for your own stable `Task`, `Run`, `Event`, `Artifact`, `Evidence`, and `Review` objects.\n - https://json-schema.org/\n\n- CloudEvents as the event envelope.\n - Gives events standard IDs, source, type, subject, time, and content type.\n - https://cloudevents.io/\n - https://github.com/cloudevents/spec\n\n- MCP for agent-to-tool and agent-to-resource access.\n - Good for issue queries, repository operations, test runners, graph lookups, and artifact retrieval.\n - It is not a complete workflow or agent-to-agent protocol.\n - https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest\n - https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/specification\n\n- A2A for remote agent discovery and agent-to-agent task exchange.\n - Use only when agents are independently deployed services; don’t require it for local subprocess workers.\n - Apache-2.0.\n - https://github.com/a2aproject/A2A\n\n- AGENTS.md for repository-local operating instructions.\n - https://agents.md/\n\n- Inspect for reproducible evaluation tasks, solvers, scorers, sandboxes, and logs.\n - Better suited to evaluations than production orchestration.\n - https://inspect.aisi.org.uk/\n - https://github.com/UKGovernmentBEIS/inspect_ai\n\n- OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions for traces and metrics.\n - https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions/tree/main/docs/gen-ai\n\nI would define the harness around an append-only event stream:\n\n```text\ntask.created\nrun.started\nagent.message\ntool.requested\ntool.completed\nartifact.produced\nevidence.attached\nreview.requested\nreview.resolved\nrun.completed\nrun.failed\n```\n\nThe critical contract is not the prompt. It is the immutable record connecting inputs, tool calls, code revision, artifacts, evidence, reviewer decisions, and final status.\n\n3. Terminal project cockpit\n\nChoose based on the implementation language:\n\n- TypeScript: OpenTUI\n - Modern TypeScript/Zig TUI library; strongest fit when the surrounding product is already TS.\n - MIT.\n - https://github.com/anomalyco/opentui\n - https://opentui.com/\n\n- Go: Bubble Tea\n - Mature Elm-style architecture with a strong component ecosystem.\n - MIT.\n - https://github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea\n\n- Python: Textual\n - Rich widgets, CSS-like styling, async operation, testing support, and terminal/web targets.\n - MIT.\n - https://github.com/Textualize/textual\n - https://textual.textualize.io/\n\nUseful public UX references:\n\n- Lazygit for pane navigation, contextual commands, and preview/detail transitions:\n https://github.com/jesseduffield/lazygit\n\n- k9s for live resource tables, drill-down, filtering, logs, command mode, and keyboard discoverability:\n https://github.com/derailed/k9s\n\nSuggested cockpit layout:\n\n```text\n┌ Projects / queues ┬ Issue or run graph ┬ Evidence / live output ┐\n│ assigned │ dependencies │ logs │\n│ blocked │ agents and runs │ diffs │\n│ awaiting review │ artifacts │ tests │\n│ recently failed │ provenance │ reviewer annotations │\n└───────────────────┴────────────────────┴────────────────────────┘\n```\n\nRecommended default combination\n\n- Plane for issue authoring and collaboration\n- PostgreSQL + Apache AGE for the authoritative company graph\n- Graphiti for optional semantic/temporal enrichment\n- JSON Schema + CloudEvents for internal contracts\n- MCP for tools/resources\n- A2A only across independently deployed agent services\n- Inspect for evaluations\n- OpenTelemetry for observability\n- OpenTUI for a TypeScript terminal cockpit\n\nThat creates a replaceable architecture: the graph, harness, agents, and cockpit share contracts without any one agent framework owning the company’s operational data.\n", ./data/llmeo/runs/bench-2026-07-31T10-05-34/raw.json:75: "exit_code": 0, ./data/llmeo/runs/bench-2026-07-31T10-05-34/raw.json:84: "stdout": "Kevin Rajan, online as `kvnloo`, describes himself as a builder, engineer, scientist, solutions architect, systems thinker, and automation-orchestration specialist.
